🤖 20 pause measurements stand; final cleanup exposed a cancellation defect

**What we did and why.** We ran the original five-second-pause baseline under enough queued work to test whether a faster pause can preserve every native request. This is a stress qualification for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality (K7), using Qwen on 16 east H100s: eight learner GPUs and eight independent inference engines. Both prospective arms use 2,048 training rows, 512 generation workers, an admission-age limit of eight updates, four concurrent sequences per engine, and forced 1,024-token training responses. The candidate has not run.

**Results.**

| Arm | Updates | Consumed loss tokens | Core seconds | Task H100 hours | Final completed score | Semantic rating | Eval truncation | Consumed age mean / p95 | Token-weight ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Original pause, failed final drain | 20 | 5,242,880 | 493.258 | 2.312793 audited for rank 0; rank 1 pending | 71/128 = 55.47%; Wilson 95% CI [46.82, 63.79]% | Not rated | 2/128 = 1.5625% | 2.202 / 7 updates | Mean 0.998550; range 0.997825–0.998854 |

All 5,120 consumed training sequences reached the forced length, and all 5,242,880 response tokens carried a loss mask. Initial raw and completed scores were both 8/128, with Wilson 95% CI [3.20, 11.85]%; final raw and completed scores were both 71/128. Initial evaluation had one length stop; final evaluation had two. These completed scores use the historical correct-answer-plus-accepted-stop definition; semantic correctness was not separately rated. No paired arm interval is available because the candidate has not yet run.

The 20 measured pauses had median 5.0999 seconds and nearest-rank p95 5.1792 seconds. Whole weight sync had median 6.2162 seconds and p95 6.3917 seconds. The audited completed-group stale-token fraction was 1,536,000 / 6,918,144 = 22.2025%, including stale-at-enqueue outcomes; this denominator excludes unfinished native work. All eight engines had real queued cohorts after the first two grace periods. Native stage coverage contains 903 events and 160 checked driver folds; per-origin CUDA durations and wall spans overlap and cannot be added into whole-sync latency.

The run then failed the frozen 30-second final idle acknowledgement. Its 3,945 request chunks reconstruct 488 receipts: initial state and all three snapshots for 20 syncs on each engine, but none of the eight required final receipts. The 29,077 native starts visible through the last recorded snapshots have matching terminal dispositions; requests resumed after those snapshots are outside that completed receipt prefix. Their final disposition is unavailable, so this is **not** a proof of whole-run conservation. W&B marks the run failed, and both the completion receipt and successful terminal manifest are absent.

The first failure was the final request-readback timeout at 19:27:09 UTC on September 8, 2026. Later metrics-endpoint connection failures occurred during teardown. Rank 0 used 1,040,757 ms on eight H100s; rank 1 is marked `cosched_failed` but still lacks a task/attempt finish timestamp. Its four-hour accounting reservation is not an observed duration or an actual-cost bound and does not delay another run. Total task cost and tokens per task H100-hour remain unresolved.

**What this means.** The workload exercises pause under a real backlog, and the final cleanup defect needs repair. The twenty measured syncs remain valid under the September 9 ruling; a final-accounting timeout after the last sync does not invalidate those measurements. A real-Ray CPU regression establishes that token-generation cancellation was not forwarded to the remote actor: the original path timed out, while routing it through the cancellation helper already used by chat stops the actor. This stress run does not establish production speedup, quality preservation, or a preferred admission-age range.

**Next.** Run the combined Snowball receiver readback and transport probe, then run the candidate with the cancellation fix and earliest first-token admission version. Keep the original baseline measurements and label the admission change when comparing the arms. Reconcile the missing task finish timestamp independently. The next milestone is completing telemetry and the pause fix (milestone 3).

Absolute correctness and paired differences are separate plot panels. Semantic ratings are unavailable for these historical dumps.

**What this means.** Cadence 4 reduced core time and weight-sync share in every observed arm, but the quality result depends strongly on objective and training seed. The large regular-objective difference on Qwen comes from a cadence-1 run whose completed answers collapsed; it does not establish a general benefit from stale data. On Snowball, quality effects change sign across seeds.

Cadence and admission-age limits changed together: Qwen compares C1/A1 with C4/A3, and Snowball compares C2/A1 with C4/A3. Token workloads also differ. These runs therefore support a partial historical comparison, not an isolated cadence effect, equal-token speedup, safe-age boundary or non-inferiority claim.

**Next.** Complete calibration and the correction comparison, then run the fixed-age cadence grid on Qwen and the post-repair Snowball grid. The next milestone remains telemetry and pause fix landed.

🤖 Historical drift indicators do not establish a safe bound across 24 windows

**What we did and why.**

Before expanding the staleness ladder, this exploratory pilot (E4.5) tested whether existing indicators warned of the next decline in completed correctness. We reused six audited 100-update Qwen runs, all with training seed 17. Each prediction uses the preceding 20 updates and predicts the change between the current evaluation and the next one. This gives 24 dependent windows: five have a decline, and three decline by more than 2 percentage points.

The feature window, risk direction and two outcome definitions were fixed before calculating associations. Completed correctness uses the same audited verifier-plus-completed-stop endpoint as the historical reports. No new training ran. This informs the goal of faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.**

| Indicator, fixed risk direction | AUROC: any next decline | AUROC: decline >2 pp |
|---|---:|---:|
| Lower legacy behavior-ratio ESS | 0.463 | 0.524 |
| Higher mean absolute log-ratio | 0.474 | 0.603 |
| Higher p99 absolute log-ratio | 0.442 | 0.619 |
| Higher mean squared log-ratio | 0.453 | 0.524 |
| Lower policy entropy | 0.547 | 0.619 |
| Higher raw gradient norm | 0.221 | 0.333 |
| Higher mean admitted age | 0.484 | 0.452 |

None of the available fixed-direction indicators reached AUROC 0.8 in this exploratory dataset. The whole-run bootstrap intervals are broad; for the primary endpoint, ESS is [0.159, 0.705], mean absolute log-ratio [0.206, 0.659], and low entropy [0.143, 0.798]. These intervals resample runs while retaining their dependent windows. They do not estimate variation across independent training seeds.

The existing ESS <0.5 flag never fired. A literal per-step mean-absolute-log-ratio >0.03 flag fired in two preceding windows; both were false alarms: 2/19, or 10.5%, for any subsequent decline. It missed all five declines. Applying the same threshold to each 20-update mean would erase both spikes, so that aggregation is reported separately.

The old worker absolute-log-ratio statistic is identically zero. Split stale-ratio ESS, split mismatch ESS, and gradient cosine are missing from these historical runs. In the new four-arm N1 correction screen, all 32 recorded stale-ESS values are exactly one, confirming that this particular statistic cannot discriminate rollout staleness when every batch has only one optimizer update.

All 7,800 native scalar values were recovered under exact run/job/region filters. Their 78 metric-family count/minimum/maximum/final summaries match the previous audited records in 312 checks. The pilot adds zero GPU-hours and zero optimizer updates; CPU analysis time was not separately benchmarked.

**What this means.**

The old indicators have not earned a predictive alert. The practical safe-bound rule is therefore closed for now: no predictive alert is adopted, and the ladders will be planned around the empirical quality knee. This is a design decision on the available evidence, not a universal statistical refutation. The held-out-seed AUROC ≥0.8 criterion remains untested; missing or structurally constant indicators remain untestable, not evidence of safety.

The legacy asynchronous behavior ratio combines engine mismatch and policy age. It must not be relabeled as either of the new split ratios. Type-A experiments need the actual split mismatch and age measurements; unit stale ESS in N1 is not a safe-bound signal. Health thresholds remain descriptive flags while the empirical quality knee and held-out-seed calibration determine the operating range.

**Next.**

Plan the staleness ladders around the empirical quality knee, with no predictive safe-bound alert. Keep the split-ratio and gradient-cosine telemetry and paired completed-score records so later held-out-seed evidence can reopen the rule. The next milestone is milestone 3, telemetry and pause fix landed.

Historical six-arm source: the audited Qwen family `2026.09.06.16`, legacy GSM8K development battery of 128 questions, greedy evaluation at 0/20/40/60/80/100. This is an exploratory reanalysis of already observed runs, not a prospective training experiment. The historical source pairs and individual receipt URIs remain bound by `async-rl-v2-e0-audit-summary.json` and its per-run provenance; the analysis does not repin old runs.

Feature means use updates `(t−20,t]` at t=20/40/60/80; outcome is completed score at t+20 minus that at t. Startup→20 is excluded because no preceding training window exists. Risk directions are fixed; thresholds are not fitted. Whole-run bootstrap: 5,000 draws, seed 20260909; draws without both labels are omitted (4,913 valid primary draws, 4,569 sensitivity draws). The held-out-seed criterion remains untested.

🤖 Two dormant correction masks stay within the observed seed noise

**What we did and why.**

For the fresh-data correction check (K12 N1), we ran eight synchronous Qwen3-0.6B updates with one optimizer update per rollout batch: behavior clipping at seeds 17 and 29, plus the off-policy mask and M2 mask at seed 17. This checks that enabling either transform leaves fresh-data updates numerically well behaved before testing stale data, toward faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. All arms used the same frozen legacy GSM8K train/dev recipe, 64 prompts × 4 responses per update, and greedy evaluation on 128 fixed questions at updates 0 and 8. Completed correctness means verifier-correct with an accepted completion stop.

**Results.**

| Arm | Final raw / completed correct | Length stops | Consumed response tokens | Core seconds | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Behavior clipping, seed 17](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/cbj0t3hi) | 70 / 70 of 128 | 4 / 128 | 316,946 | 79.330 | 1.606573 |

Both masks removed exactly zero tokens in the reported update metrics, and M2's pre-mask squared log-ratio statistic was zero. All four arms completed eight successful optimizer updates with positive gradients; each retained all 14 correction fields in both the batch aggregate and update-specific W&B records. The minimum raw gradient norm across the arms was 0.75685. These correction fields describe the last microbatch and rank mean; they are not token-pooled fractions for the whole update.

The frozen engineering noise band was the absolute difference between the two behavior-clipping seeds: 3/128, or 2.34375 percentage points. The off-policy mask differed from seed 17 by +1.5625 pp, with a paired 97.5% interval of [−4.6875, +7.8125] pp. M2 differed by −0.78125 pp, with [−8.59375, +7.03125] pp. Both meet the absolute noise-band rule. The four runs used 6.476078 task H100-hours. All eight GPU tasks succeeded on their sole scheduler attempt. Retained hub logs contain no startup port-retry messages, but the incomplete telemetry coverage below prevents a whole-job zero-engine-death claim.

**What this means.**

The fresh-data numerical and final-score checks pass. This is an engineering check, not a non-inferiority result or a ranking of corrections. Zero masking here does not prove an active masking formula: the separate native numerical fixtures supplied that proof with nonzero retained gradients and actual parameter changes.

The central query currently returns 23 of the expected 32 source-order events and eight of the expected 16 role-terminal receipts; every available terminal reports zero lost records. A direct regional query found neither the semantic training namespace nor its legacy parent namespace. This establishes a retrieval gap, not a correction or exporter failure. No full native telemetry gate or matched source-order union proof has been asserted.

**Next.**

Run a separately labeled eight-updates-per-batch M2 mechanism diagnostic using the numerical and fresh-data checks established here, with its own native coverage checks. The comparison of its full prompt set against all eight fresh-data batches remains unqualified while those source vectors are missing. The historical indicator pilot now supports planning the ladders around the empirical quality knee. The next milestone remains telemetry and pause fix landed.

🤖 Two training seeds differ by 8.61 points on completed heldout answers

**What we did and why.** We measured evaluation and training-seed variation
before using small-model experiments to choose faster Snowball training at
the same answer quality. Two Qwen anchors trained for 96 updates on the
frozen 1,918-question training view, then exported actual checkpoint weights.
Each checkpoint received five greedy passes on 256 development questions,
a separate greedy heldout pass, and separate stochastic panels with one,
four and eight draws on all 2,009 heldout questions.

**Results.**

| Anchor training seed | Heldout K8 completed | Pointwise 95% interval | Semantic correct / resolved | Semantic unresolved | Contract–semantic disagreements | Dev questions changing across five greedy passes |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 17 | 6,842 / 16,072 = 42.57% | 40.91–44.23% | 10,944 / 15,968 | 104 | 4,189 | 21 / 256 |
| 29 | 8,225 / 16,072 = 51.18% | 49.55–52.81% | 10,948 / 15,888 | 184 | 2,799 | 24 / 256 |

The paired difference is 8.61 percentage points, with a pointwise interval
of 7.56–9.65 points. These are large-question normal intervals conditional on
these two trained checkpoints, with each question's eight responses kept
together. They do not cover uncertainty over future training seeds.
The Platinum component contributes 2,606 versus 4,087 completed responses
out of 9,672; the MATH component contributes 4,236 versus 4,138 out of 6,400.

All 58,812 response rows across the two checkpoints passed exact native
token, request, renderer and contract-metric audits. Training, export and
calibration used 14.53 task H100-hours combined; evaluation alone used 0.635.

The balanced seed-by-question decomposition on the stochastic eight-draw
panel gives variance components 0.003688 for training seed, 0.112529 for
question, 0.013637 for their interaction and 0.121076 for draw residuals.
All raw estimates are positive. Seed variance has only one degree of freedom.

Under the explicit assumption that those marginal components apply equally
to two future arms, two training seeds and 2,009 questions with eight draws
give the following endpoint MDE planning sensitivity for the prespecified
45-contrast correction family, at 80% power and two-sided familywise 5% error:

| Assumed correlation of each component between future arms | Planning MDE |
| --- | ---: |
| −1 | 35.83 pp |
| 0, primary assumption | 25.34 pp |
| 0.5 | 17.92 pp |
| 0.9 | 8.01 pp |

The full artifact retains every componentwise correlation combination,
all raw and truncated moments, and the smaller prespecified comparison
families. These are normal planning approximations, not certified power
or confidence limits on the MDE. The endpoint calculation does not establish
power for a four-arm difference in age degradation.

**What this means.** The earlier rough five-point MDE is not supported by this
calibration under the stated assumptions. Similar development scores did
not predict heldout contract stability; the near-equal semantic totals and
large Platinum contract gap remain visible rather than being collapsed
into one quality score. Repeated greedy decoding also changed some answers.
The two-seed estimate is too uncertain to certify a two-point non-inferiority
claim, and the evaluation contract remains unchanged.

**Next.** Start the exploratory staleness calibration with matched control and
perturbation seeds to measure paired differences under its actual runner and
ordering. A large planning MDE does not stop that calibration; it limits which
rankings or quality guarantees the results can support. Snowball system
qualification and the frozen difficulty measurements continue independently.
The written disagreement sample remains available for review before any pool change.

**What we did and why.** We tested the communication path that sends updated trainer weights to rollout workers, a prerequisite for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. Two Ray actors on separate H100s each retained its own singleton default process group, then joined a shared custom NCCL group through the production initializer. 🤖 Milestone 3: telemetry and the pause fix are integrated

**What we did and why.** We qualified request accounting and shorter pauses when syncing updated weights to rollout workers, so later experiments can measure asynchronous training without losing requests or confusing policy versions. The candidate completed twenty measured syncs on Qwen, using the earliest first-token policy version across partial rollouts. It also finished its final drain successfully.

Native optimizer remainder qualification (K29) landed: the synthetic two-GPU test saved about 4 retained bytes per owned parameter with BF16 moments and about 6 with moments plus remainders; all tested same-geometry checkpoint continuations were exact. Full-model memory and learning remain to be measured.

**Results.** The measured pause comparison was:

| Measurement | Recorded baseline | Candidate |
|---|---:|---:|
| Median pause | 5.100 s | 0.107 s |
| Median complete weight sync | 6.216 s | 1.211 s |
| Core time over twenty updates | 493.258 s | 433.487 s |

The candidate's pause p95 was 0.171 s and its maximum was 0.295 s, passing the median-below-0.3-second gate. All 29,344 started requests have terminal dispositions; eight engine identities stayed stable across the twenty measured syncs. These are descriptive timings from one matched configuration and seed, without an inferential timing interval. The baseline's failure during final cleanup remains recorded; its twenty measured syncs remain valid. The candidate changes both pause handling and admission-version selection, so the comparison does not isolate their individual effects or establish equal answer quality.

The candidate ended with 65/128 correct, completed development answers versus 71/128 in the baseline: a paired difference of −4.69 pp, 95% interval [−12.50, +3.13] pp. This question-resampling interval is conditional on one observed training seed and does not establish the two-point non-inferiority requirement. Both arms consumed 5,242,880 response tokens under the forced-length stress setup.

Since the evaluation and task milestone:

- The [seeded runner control](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5590472277) matched consumed prompt-set fingerprints and raw rewards at all eight updates. Its age-zero async arm was slower, and its completed-answer interval did not establish two-point non-inferiority.
- [Checkpoint calibration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5599222212) audited 58,812 responses. The two anchors differed by 8.61 pp [7.56, 9.65] on expected completed correctness across eight draws. That interval conditions on those checkpoints; the future-arm planning model's 25.34 pp minimum detectable effect exposes limited seed-level precision, with only one seed degree of freedom.
- The [full initial Snowball ratings](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5598262769), following the [pilot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5590578846), measured 40.24% [39.10, 41.37] completed correctness across 12,000 responses. This describes the selected 3,000-question panel at one checkpoint. Fresh ratings of the extremes and task selection are still underway.
- The [indicator pilot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5598170776) found no available fixed-direction indicator reaching AUROC 0.8 across its 24 dependent windows. No predictive alert is adopted; the ladders will locate the empirical quality knee.
- The [historical cadence reanalysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5598140083) found lower core time at cadence four, but Snowball's completed-answer effects changed sign across seeds. Cadence, admission limits and token workloads changed together, so this does not isolate a cadence effect.
- The [fresh-data correction check](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5598381936) found both masks dormant over eight updates, with no established quality benefit. Missing native source vectors and terminal receipts still prevent its full matched source-order qualification.
- The [eight-updates-per-batch correction diagnostic](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5599565967) demonstrated active masking with positive gradients and complete native coverage. Its averaged diagnostics are not whole-update token fractions, and it does not supply the missing matched quality comparison.
- The [same-host transport diagnostic](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5599467859) passed nine transfers and eighteen rank-level byte checks. Inter-host performance and equality of weights installed in the receiver model remain separate qualifications.

**What this means.** The request-accounting and pause changes are ready for this program's next asynchronous experiments. They remove the measured long pause without losing request dispositions in the qualified run. They do not establish Snowball speed, a safe off-policy age, or non-inferior quality. The calibration and indicator results make the confirmation work essential: uncertainty must be measured across training seeds, and constant or missing indicators cannot certify safety.

**Next.** Complete the fresh Snowball ratings and disagreement review, finish the reuse-ladder evaluations, and qualify receiver readback and inter-host transport for the next weight-sync improvements. The next milestone is **4, answer contract and tasks fixed**.

**What we did and why.** We qualified the production custom process-group path (K10 transport precursor) between two native Ray GPU actors on distinct physical hosts. The launcher repair supplies the immutable runtime root; the scientific packet remains three repeats at each of 32, 128 and 512 MiB, with aligned communicator settings and batch invariance off.

**Results.** Both tasks succeeded on their first attempts. The nine sender/receiver pairs produce 18 matching payload receipts, and each native rank checks every byte against its known pattern. Independent CPU replay recomputes all expected hashes. Both custom/default groups are destroyed, 30 origin-preserving stage events are retained, and both hosts report IB with GPU-direct RDMA.

This establishes the transport precursor only. It does not prove full-model byte identity, receiver layout/headroom, packed-buffer performance or a Snowball speedup.

**Next.** Use the Snowball zero-update receiver readback to qualify the actual expert layout and available memory, then connect the bounded bucket implementation and frozen-sender byte replay. The next weight-sync milestone requires the full-model correctness and latency gates.

🤖 Two updates per batch preserve more completed answers at update 96

**What we did and why.** We compared one versus two policy updates per rollout batch in the first four Qwen3-0.6B reuse-ladder runs (E4.1), using training seeds 17 and 29. Each run completed 96 successful optimizer updates and consumed 6,144 prompt groups, with four responses per group. We exported the actual checkpoints and evaluated each on the same 2,009 held-out questions. The primary score averages completed correctness over eight stochastic responses per question and then equally across the two observed seeds; it is not best-of-eight.

**Results.** Two updates per batch achieved **46.22% completed correctness**, versus **15.49%** for one update. The paired difference is **+30.73 percentage points**, with conditional **98.75% interval [29.26, 32.21]**. The two seed-specific differences are +32.97 and +28.49 points. The interval retains the predeclared four-contrast correction even though only this first contrast is reported.

| Held-out endpoint, both seeds combined | One update per batch | Two updates per batch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Completed correctness | 4,980 / 32,144 (15.49%) | 14,858 / 32,144 (46.22%) |
| Verifier correctness, regardless of stopping | 17,196 / 32,144 (53.50%) | 16,020 / 32,144 (49.84%) |
| Accepted stop | 6,596 / 32,144 (20.52%) | 28,041 / 32,144 (87.24%) |
| Mean raw reward | 0.344232 | 0.362152 |
| Semantic correct / semantically resolved | 16,725 / 25,073 | 21,152 / 30,951 |
| Semantically unresolved responses | 7,071 | 1,193 |
| Contract–semantic disagreements among resolved responses | 3,858 | 5,997 |

Raw reward retains the task's original signed or task-native scale and is not the ranking metric. Semantic results use Math-Verify and the qualified extraction contract; unresolved responses are shown explicitly, not counted as correct or silently dropped into an accuracy claim. Counts span repeated responses to 2,009 questions, not 32,144 independent questions.

The development decline appears before the final checkpoint: the one-update runs fall from 151/256 and 152/256 completed answers at update 64 to 38/256 and 20/256 at update 96. Their final development truncation is 82.42% and 91.41%; both two-update runs finish at 168/256, with truncation 15.23% and 8.59%.

| Training configuration / seed | Updates | Consumed response tokens | Scoped training-step seconds | Training H100-hours | Token-weighted age mean / p95 | Mean stale ESS |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| One update / 17 | 96 | 7,388,288 | 859.763 | 5.400462 | 0 / 0 | 1.000000 |
| One update / 29 | 96 | 8,884,347 | 877.884 | 5.474991 | 0 / 0 | 1.000000 |
| Two updates / 17 | 96 | 5,324,998 | 688.390 | 4.577489 | 0.4975 / 1 | 0.999109 |
| Two updates / 29 | 96 | 5,890,801 | 688.012 | 4.725169 | 0.5000 / 1 | 0.971320 |

Dedicated core time and clipped-token entropy are unavailable in this frozen runtime. The scoped seconds cover generation through weight sync, excluding startup, evaluation, checkpoint callbacks and loader iteration; they are not substituted for core time. All four training runs together used 20.178111 H100-hours, their exports 1.622133, and the nine-panel evaluations 2.287262. These phases are counted once each. All GPU tasks succeeded on their first attempts. The native exporter was configured with zero retries despite its outer envelope requesting one; that reporting mismatch is being repaired before further exports and does not change these successful-attempt costs.

**What this means.** The two-update configuration preserves substantially more usable completed answers on this held-out battery in both observed seeds. Verifier correctness alone reverses the ordering, showing why the accepted-stop requirement matters. The ESS statistic is structurally one for one-update batches, so it cannot warn about that configuration's late decline.

This comparison changes the whole reuse configuration: rollout batch size and concurrency, token work and source exposure differ. One-update epochs drop 62 rows and two-update epochs drop 126; consumed source order diverges after group 1,792. We therefore do not attribute the gain to stale age alone or claim equal-token speedup. The interval resamples paired questions conditional on two observed training seeds; it does not establish population-seed non-inferiority. The full ladder knee remains unknown, and adjusted p-values await the complete four-contrast family.

**Next.** Evaluate the remaining verified reuse checkpoints and complete the missing training arm, retaining their actual lifecycle defects separately from scientific evidence. In parallel, decompose Snowball's retained nontermination failures and complete task selection. The next milestone is **4: answer contract and tasks fixed**.

🤖 All 128 final responses hit the length limit in the importance-sampling run

## What we did and why

We audited the retained Snowball development responses from three 100-update runs to separate observable parser, stopping-configuration and repetition issues before testing remedies (E6.1 stage 1). This was a CPU analysis of existing data, covering 18 checkpoints and 2,304 responses. It launched no new training.

Each response was decoded with the pinned tokenizer and checked against its retained text and token hashes. We located the scorer's first numeric answer marker relative to the actual thinking-token state, including the prompt's opening state. The repetition diagnostic is the fraction of consecutive 16-token windows that duplicate an earlier window. The primary threshold is 0.5, with sensitivity checks at 0.25 and 0.75. These diagnostics overlap; they are not a partition of causes.

## Results

At update 100, the results were:

| Run | Responses at the length limit | First answer marker inside thinking, among length-limited responses | Repetition diagnostic ≥ 0.5, among length-limited responses |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Weight sync every two updates, maximum age one | 63/128 | 58/63 (92.1%) | 62/63 (98.4%) |
| Weight sync every four updates, maximum age three | 25/128 | 19/25 (76.0%) | 24/25 (96.0%) |
| Every four updates, maximum age three, truncated importance sampling | 128/128 | 117/128 (91.4%) | 128/128 (100%) |

The older raw scorer rewarded 56, 16 and 113 length-limited responses in these three final checkpoints. Every one of those rewarded, length-limited responses had both its first answer marker inside thinking and a repetition diagnostic of at least 0.5. These are raw scorer outcomes, not completed-answer correctness.

The repetition finding persists across the prespecified sensitivity thresholds. At 0.25, all length-limited responses qualify. At 0.75, the counts are 41/63, 18/25 and 91/128. Across all final responses, first answer markers occur inside thinking in 123/128, 122/128 and 117/128; the parser issue is therefore also present outside the length-limited subset.

The effective EOS configuration was present for all three runs. The pinned backend defaults to respecting EOS, uses tokenizer EOS 128001, and adds generation-config EOS 128009. Executing its actual configuration-update method reproduces that effective stop set; switching `ignore_eos` on removes both stopping conditions. An empty explicit stop-token list does not establish a missing EOS stop set. This is a configuration diagnostic, not a causal explanation of individual truncations.

## What this means

The raw scorer can reward an answer marker still inside thinking, including responses that repeat until their length limit. Repetition and answers parsed inside thinking frequently coexist. The audit cannot assign either as the sole cause of truncation, and it does not establish that EOS configuration was broken.

The evidence uses finalized trajectory tokens. It does not reconstruct unavailable raw engine outputs. These deterministic development responses describe the observed runs; they do not estimate training-seed uncertainty or held-out quality, and they do not qualify a remedy.

## Next

Prepare the prescribed short Snowball remedy comparison: parser correction alone and its combinations with forced thinking closure, the two truncation penalties, and repetition stopping. Preserve the existing stopping settings unless an effective-configuration defect is demonstrated. Stage 2 remains necessary for milestone 4; this CPU audit does not complete that milestone or establish non-inferiority.

The preceding attempt ran twice and failed before the first sync because the diagnostic incorrectly expected all eight DP cores inside each of eight separate actors. The sampled digest matches are diagnostic evidence, not full-model bit identity, and the free-memory readings do not establish the later transfer or PPO peak. The optional grouped-allocation attribute was unavailable; that separate optimization remains unqualified. InfiniBand evidence is retained in bounded log tails, including GDRDMA lines for 34 processes, rather than a complete fabric trace.

**Next.** Run one packed installation and an untimed full frozen-source byte replay, retaining complete sender/receiver coverage and measured additional allocation. **What we did and why.** We screened two correction objectives on Qwen3-0.6B before using them in studies of faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The screen compares a token-ratio mask and a second-moment mask with behavior clipping, using a second baseline seed to define the prespecified screening band. Each arm made eight optimizer updates; a separate second-moment diagnostic used eight minibatches from one larger rollout batch. This is class R research: the correction-selection experiment decides eventual use (K12).

**Results.**

| Arm | Updates | Consumed tokens | Core s | Task H100 h | Completed | Semantic | Eval truncation % | Group age mean / p95 | Stale ESS range |

Completed correctness means full credit from the task's own scorer and an accepted stop. The baseline seeds differ by 3 answers out of 256, fixing the absolute screening band at 1.171875 percentage points. Token masking differs from the seed-17 baseline by +1.171875 pp, with paired 97.5% CI [−3.90625, 6.25], and meets that band exactly. Second-moment masking differs by −1.953125 pp, CI [−7.03125, 3.125], and fails it. These question-bootstrap intervals condition on the observed seed, use 50,000 draws and cover the two candidate comparisons; they do not establish non-inferiority or a population-level seed effect.

Every arm consumed 512 distinct prompt groups. The matched seed-17 arms use the same source-group union, but generated responses and token counts differ. The eight-minibatch diagnostic partitions 512 distinct groups across eight optimizer minibatches; it does not replay the same tokens eight times. Its 434,939 tokens are unique consumed response-token work. This is not a matched timing or endpoint-quality comparison with the one-minibatch arms. Its native positive masked fraction at minibatch index 5 is 0.0005154639366082847. The recorded second moment falls from 0.02274983562529087 to 0.01772126741707325 there. These are last-microbatch, rank-mean telemetry values: being below the 0.04 threshold after rank averaging does not mean that no rank applied masking.

All ten original physical tasks succeeded. The audit verifies 14,871 scalar joins, 33 exact integer digest joins, 40 optimizer events and all 20 role-terminal records with zero lost or queued records. Core seconds sum the training-step timer around generation, training and weight sync, excluding evaluation and startup. All 33 native phase-duration records match W&B within 1.8e-15 seconds of JSON serialization round-off. These are two records of the same timer, not independent clock measurements. Stale ESS is identically one in the one-minibatch arms by construction, not evidence that engine mismatch is absent. Semantic rescoring was not part of this small development gate.

**What this means.** Keep token masking available behind its disabled-by-default flag for the planned correction comparison. The second-moment candidate fails this frozen screen and remains unqualified; the band is not widened and the failed arm is not rerun to obtain a pass. Both candidate comparisons also change the base objective from behavior clipping to regular PPO, so neither isolates the causal effect of its correction alone. The diagnostic establishes that masking can activate, not that it improves quality.

**Next.** Complete the admission-delay qualification before the full staleness report and correction-selection study. A causal second-moment comparison would need a newly frozen, matched regular-objective control under the new screening geometry. These steps lead toward the milestone “correction chosen and safe-bound rule”; the intervening system work continues toward “weight sync cut at least fourfold with bit-identical proof.”

🤖 Seeded release thresholds leave mean training age unchanged at 3.0

**What we did and why.** We tested whether deliberately holding generated prompt groups makes training consume older responses, a prerequisite for measuring how staleness affects faster Snowball training at the same answer quality (K17). Two Qwen3-0.6B arms used the same seed, eight updates, FIFO admission, publication every four updates, an age limit of six, a 256-group buffer and 64 generation workers. One arm had no injected delay; the other set each prompt’s release threshold to its first-token admission step plus a reproducible integer from zero to three. This threshold may already have passed when generation finishes; it does not guarantee additional waiting after completion. Admission order and delay are class T tradeoffs: this test does not select a default.

**Results.**

| Arm | Updates | Consumed tokens | Core s | Task H100 h | Final completed | Semantic | Eval truncation % | Group age mean / p95 | Stale ESS range |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---:|---|---|
| FIFO, no injected delay | 8 | 433,471 | 63.12 | 1.737556 | 107/256 (41.80%) | Not separately scored | 3.91 | 3.0 / 6 | 1.0000 |
| FIFO, seeded delay 0–3 | 8 | 434,728 | 64.60 | 1.979604 | 106/256 (41.41%) | Not separately scored | 5.08 | 3.0 / 6 | 1.0000 |

The frozen capability requirement was a positive increase in mean group age. The observed increase is **0.0 updates, so that gate fails**. Both arms have the identical age histogram: 64 groups at each age 0, 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, and 128 at age 3. Each consumed 320 groups older than two updates. Token-weighted mean ages are 3.2300 and 3.1455, respectively; these also do not show an increase from delay.

The delay mechanism itself executed: the 512 consumed groups received delays 0/1/2/3 in counts 150/140/107/115. Every consumed UID joins to its seeded assignment and first-token admission stamp; no group was released before its assigned real update, and no consumed age exceeded six. Both arms generated 832 groups: 512 consumed, 64 cancelled before enqueue and 256 discarded at epoch end, with zero stale discards and complete token conservation. Under this schedule, delay changed which prompts entered batches without changing the consumed policy-age cohorts.

Completed correctness is full credit from the task's own scorer multiplied by an accepted stop, computed from the final 256 retained response records. Descriptive endpoint Wilson 95% intervals are 35.92–47.92% and 35.54–47.52%. These reused development questions had a 1,024-token response limit. The two endpoints are descriptive; no paired quality superiority, non-inferiority or default-selection test was performed.

The displayed stale ESS compares the training forward pass with the pre-update current-policy forward pass. With one optimizer update per batch, its value of one does not establish that old rollout behavior matches the current policy. The separate current-policy-versus-rollout ESS ranges are 0.99656–0.99927 and 0.99686–0.99933; those comparisons combine age and inference-engine effects rather than isolating either one.

All four original physical tasks succeeded, costing 3.717160 H100 hours. The audit joins 6,768 native/W&B scalars, 16 exact source digests and all eight role-terminal records, with zero lost or queued records. All 16 native core phase durations match W&B within 8.9e-16 seconds of JSON round-off. Core time includes buffer wait, training and scheduled weight publication, excluding evaluation, checkpoint callbacks and startup; generation overlaps this window. These are two recordings of the same timer, not independent clocks or a matched-token speed comparison.

**What this means.** Keep the failed positive-shift result unchanged and leave the delay capability unqualified. Mechanical release correctness is established, but it does not establish the intended age shift. This pair also does not resolve the larger staleness ladder: its publication cadence and common buffer geometry differ from that fleet, and it has no held-out quality comparison.

**Next.** Resolve the proposed comparator geometry before further native execution. The CPU schedule study found that the original freshest-first comparator at cadence four and age limit three cannot produce its required stale discards because each policy cohort drains before publication; a fresh three-arm comparison at age limit six is awaiting the explicit geometry ruling. Qualification would then support the larger staleness study and the milestone “correction chosen and safe-bound rule.”

🤖 Packed Snowball broadcast takes 18.87 seconds and misses the halving target

**What we did and why.** We compared the reference weight publication with a packed 1 GiB-buffer implementation on Snowball, with 32 training GPUs and 8 inference GPUs per arm. This class X transport experiment aims to make training faster while installing exactly the same weights (K8/K14). Each completed arm ran 20 updates and 20 measured publications, with a separate frozen-sender byte replay after each installation. The original candidate attempt failed during model staging before any measurement; the repaired attempt completed.

**Results.**

| Measured duration | Reference median | Packed median |
|---|---:|---:|
| Weight broadcast | 20.52 s | 18.87 s |
| Whole diagnostic weight sync, including byte replay | 52.98 s | 49.65 s |
| Gate-only full-byte replay | 31.38 s | 29.51 s |
| Pause RPC | 0.2006 s | 0.1934 s |

Broadcast ranged from 19.21–23.01 seconds for the reference and 18.03–20.89 seconds for the packed arm. These are observed ranges over 20 publications, not confidence intervals. There is one completed run per arm; repeated publications within a run do not establish a replicated speedup interval. The packed/reference median ratio is 0.9196. The predeclared target was at most 7.478 seconds, half the historical 14.96-second baseline, so the latency gate failed.

| Run accounting | Reference | Packed, repaired attempt |
|---|---:|---:|
| Updates | 20 | 20 |
| Consumed loss tokens | 3,139,880 | 3,371,287 |
| Recorded core seconds | 1,760 | 1,703 |
| Task H100-hours | 27.04 | 26.06 |

The different consumed-token totals and diagnostic replay overhead make these core-time totals unsuitable for a production throughput claim. Completed correctness, semantic scores and their paired intervals are not qualified by this transport audit; no quality ranking or non-inferiority claim is made.

Both arms passed the full installed-byte and bounded-memory checks across all publications: 134,157,778,944 logical wire bytes, zero receiver mismatches, 40 distinct GPUs and five original task attempts per arm. Peak additional replay scratch was 512 bytes on a sender and 852,480 bytes on a receiver. Logical wire bytes are not NIC egress measurements. The pause number is the pause RPC, not the full time inference remained paused.

The failed staging attempt contributes 0.2882 known task H100-hours, but four sibling tasks lack finish timestamps. Total experiment-group GPU-hours therefore remain incomplete; the two completed-arm totals above exclude that failed attempt. Model staging took 213.5–217.5 seconds per node for the reference and 180.5–191.9 seconds for the repaired candidate.

**What this means.** Byte correctness is established for this diagnostic, but packing alone did not produce the required latency reduction. This class X candidate is not ready for default adoption. The expensive replay is a gate-only check outside the broadcast interval; its removal must not be counted as a production transport improvement. Missing per-sync publication-stage events in the packed arm are expected; replay and synchronization-begin timings come from W&B/stdout rather than Finelog phase-duration rows.

**Next.** A 2 GiB buffer follow-up is running. In parallel we are preparing overlapping export, transfer and installation and the expert-block broadcast topology, with H100 measurement packets and independent byte/memory audits. The next performance milestone is weight sync cut by at least fourfold with bit-identical proof.

**What we did and why.** Overlapping export, transfer and installation could reduce Snowball's weight-sync time while preserving installed weights exactly. We then tested CUDA connection counts of 1 and 8, crossed with streaming allocation and a preallocated source pool, using four fresh process pairs on the same two H100s. Each pair ran serial and pipeline modes through the actual sender/receiver code with synthetic tensors; no model or dataset was loaded.

| CUDA connections | Source allocation | Serial export/send overlap | Pipeline export/send overlap | Serial receive/load overlap | Pipeline receive/load overlap |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | Streaming | 0 ms | 0 ms | 0 ms | 0 ms |

Receiver overlap also appears in serial mode at eight connections because the receiver already uses separate streams; that observation alone does not establish the new sender pipeline's benefit.

These values are intersections of measured CUDA stream-stage intervals for four 256 MiB tensors, not isolated kernel busy time or Snowball latency. issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Marin cannot run FinanceBench or SimpleQA with a Together-backed judge without replacing or exposing candidate-endpoint credentials. A direct Together probe confirmed that `openai/gpt-oss-120b` supports the Chat Completions API used by FinanceBench and the Responses API request shape used by SimpleQA, so provider compatibility is not the blocker.

Reproduce:
1. Launch FinanceBench with a distinct external judge credential. [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/93251781092fa281077dff0a9c7b455fd6cc9677/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L229-L235) overwrites `OPENAI_API_KEY` with `local-endpoint` in the Evalchemy child.
2. Launch a supplied Harbor SimpleQA policy whose verifier requires a separate provider key. [`HarborDefinition.secret_env_for`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/93251781092fa281077dff0a9c7b455fd6cc9677/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L117-L120) resolves only the Daytona credential, so the isolated verifier does not receive the judge key.
3. Observe that FinanceBench cannot authenticate to the judge and SimpleQA has no verifier credential. Passing the Together key as the process-wide `OPENAI_API_KEY` would also send a judge credential through the candidate client boundary.

Expected: Evalchemy judges and Harbor verifiers receive explicit provider key, base URL, and model settings at verifier-only boundaries. Candidate endpoint authentication remains unchanged. Judge transport and parsing failures fail evaluation coverage instead of becoming incorrect answers.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Architecture and plan for the evaldash issues, peer-reviewed as requested: https://loom.oa.dev/s/m6bfst8b/artifacts/evaldash-stats-engine (rev 2)

The four subissues are the same gap seen from four angles. Evaldash has no representation of *a measurement and how much of it happened* — a matrix cell is `value: float | None`, so there is nowhere to put "236 of 240 intended trials, 4 agent timeouts", and nothing to filter or aggregate on except presence. #8084 needs that representation to admit a partial run, #8085 needs it to qualify an aggregate, #8086 needs it to decide which result is admissible, #8087 needs a query object over it.

So the pre-work is one engine, shared by the eval runners and the dashboard: a typed measurement carrying its item counts and interval, plus an explicit selection query over a set of measurements. Each issue is then a call into it.

**Statistical core.** One estimand: the success rate over the items a run set out to grade. With `c = n_scored / n_attempted`, θ splits into an identified part and an unidentified one, and the missing part gets bounded rather than imputed — missingness correlates with task difficulty, which is exactly why #8084 needs a gate rather than an average. The reported interval is Wilson on the scored items, scaled by `c` and widened by `1 − c`, with an Imbens–Manski critical value so it covers the parameter at 95% instead of over-covering at ~97.5%. Width is at least `1 − c`: a run that graded 92.3% of its trials reports an interval at least 7.7 points wide however many trials it ran.

**Three things fall out that are worth flagging before implementation.**

1. Harbor already publishes a biased number, and the gate would expose it. `_aggregate` divides by `len(trials)` while an errored trial is read back with reward 0.0, so `accuracy` scores every timeout as a wrong answer — the Manski lower bound, computed by accident and labelled a point estimate. It is masked today only because any failed trial aborts the run. Relaxing that without fixing the denominator would ship the bias. The intended-trial count also cannot come from the result glob: a trial that dies before writing leaves no file, so the runs with the worst attrition would report perfect coverage.
2. Ranking cannot use `k / n_scored`. It is a complete-case estimate, so ranking on it rewards a model for timing out on hard items — #8085's complaint re-entering through the sort key. Ranking uses the interval's lower bound. At `c = 1` the two coincide, so the 368 evalchemy runs are unaffected.
3. A 90% gate admits results for display but cannot support ordering claims. Resolving a 5-point gap between two models needs coverage above 0.975 on both, and 2 points needs 0.99. Display admission and comparison admission are two thresholds, not one.

**Evidence.** Everything above is checked against the 387 records under `gs://marin-eval-metadata/evals` (CoreWeave needs credentials this session did not have). Item counts are already there — 1204 of 1249 per-task metric dicts carry `sample_len`, and Harbor carries `total`/`solved` — so the primary adapter is the record, not the archive, which matters because only 6 of 387 runs have a finestore archive today. A cross-check worth knowing about: the llama-3.1-8b mmlu record has 124 task entries because the run wrote the whole 62-entry panel twice, once under `mmlu_5shot` and once under a task directory named `tmp6jnnx8cc`, scoring 0.63502 and 0.63488. Benchmark identity cannot be the raw evalchemy task directory, and that duplicate looks like a separate launcher bug.

**Peer review** changed the design materially, so the artifact records it. Adopted: the Imbens–Manski correction; asymmetric difference bounds; demoting paired comparison, which provably buys zero attrition-width reduction; the Harbor denominator fixes; dropping a fleet-max denominator inference and a new Postgres table that would have been write-only; and moving the engine out of `lib/finestore` — `marin-core` already depends on `marin-finestore`, so an engine there naming `RunStatus` would create a distribution cycle and break that wheel's CI leg. It lives in `marin/evaluation/` under the same import-light contract as `records.py` and is vendored into the dashboard image by one `COPY`; "on top of finestore" holds on the data path, not the package path. One of my own claims did not survive: the apparent mmlu panel drift between models was my triple-count of group and leaf rows.

Proceeding to implementation as one PR: engine and tests, the record coverage contract, the Harbor gate, the evaldash panel API, then the SPA. Item-level tallies, paired comparison intervals, and evidence-based suspect-zero detection are deferred and will be filed separately.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Plan and first PR are up.

**Artifact (architecture + plan, peer-reviewed twice):** https://loom.oa.dev/s/m6bfst8b/artifacts/evaldash-stats-engine
**PR:** #8122 — CI green.

## What the four issues have in common

evaldash had no representation of *a measurement and how much of it happened* — a cell was `value: float | None`. That single gap produces all four symptoms: a Harbor batch with one timed-out trial in 240 is either discarded or silently scored as if the trial were wrong (#8084); a cross-benchmark mean is reported without saying which benchmarks, at which metric, or what it did about the ones a model never ran (#8085); a partial re-run hides older results that are still the newest available for their own benchmark (#8086); and filtering has nowhere to express "complete coverage only" because coverage isn't a thing the data carries (#8087).

So the PR is mostly the engine, with the four issues as applications of it — the pre-work-plus-applications shape you suggested, in one PR rather than five.

## The engine

Each result is stored as sufficient statistics (items graded, items attempted, correct count, recorded dispersion, per-cause counts of ungraded items) and intervals are derived on read. The estimand is θ over the items a run *set out* to grade. With `c = n_scored / n_attempted`, `θ = c·θ_obs + (1−c)·θ_miss`, and θ_miss is bounded to [0, 1] rather than imputed — a trial that times out is more likely to be a hard trial, so imputing anything for it is a guess about difficulty. The interval therefore widens by at least `1−c`: admitting a partial batch costs width proportional to what was missed, which is your "unknown interval around the missed answers" made concrete.

Two details worth flagging:

- The critical value is Imbens–Manski, not the ordinary 1.96. Applying the two-sided quantile to an interval that already spans an unidentified region covers the identified *set* at 95% and over-covers the parameter (~97.5% at realistic coverage rates). Because Δ is known exactly here rather than estimated, the usual objection to that correction doesn't apply.
- Binary metrics use Wilson, because eval results really do sit at the boundary — 0 of 8 agentic trials has a normal interval of *zero width* and a Wilson interval of [0.000, 0.324].

Every ordering in the system sorts on the interval's lower bound, so losing items cannot buy rank.

## Per issue

**#8084** — Harbor takes its attempted-trial count from the job's own bookkeeping (counting result files misses every trial that died before writing one, so preempted runs would report perfect coverage), divides rates by the trials a verifier actually graded, and keeps the per-error-type counts of the rest. A batch below a 90% completion gate fails as `infra_failed` and still records its coverage, so the rejection reads as counts. Run detail shows the breakdown. An unreadable job record leaves the count *unknown* rather than equal to results-found — the runs where it's unknown are exactly the interrupted ones a found-count would certify as complete.

**#8085** — No cross-benchmark mean is shown at all unless a caller names a missing-data policy, and one that is shown renders its panel, per-benchmark metrics, and policy inline. The primary surface is a panel table: one row per model, one column per benchmark. `ComparePage`'s client-side mean, which scored a missing shared benchmark as 0, is gone; comparison goes through the engine and answers orderings with a difference interval per benchmark rather than two error bars to eyeball.

**#8086** — Each benchmark comes from the newest run that clears the request's admission rules, across cohorts, so a partial re-run no longer hides results still newest for their own benchmark. `cohort=` pins to one launch when you want that instead. Every cell carries its run id, version, git sha, and timestamp; a `(model, benchmark)` with no admitted cell reports why and links the offending run, so an empty cell is explained rather than blank.

**#8087** — Benchmark column selection, a one-action complete-panel filter, cohort selection, model search, and run-metadata facets (accelerator/platform/backend/mechanism/user) are all in the request, so a panel is a shareable URL. The active ones render as removable chips: a number on screen should never be the product of a filter the reader can't see.

## Deliberately not in this PR

Filed as follow-ups: item-level tallies so binary intervals stop depending on inverting a rate (#8123), paired comparisons on shared items (#8124), the evalchemy launcher writing the same mmlu panel under two task directories (#8125), attempted-item counts for lm-eval runs so their intervals stop being sampling-only (#8126), and pyrefly/test-selection coverage for the evaldash server tree (#8127).

One caveat on #8126 worth knowing before reading the dashboard: today nearly every evalchemy run's interval is labelled `sampling_only`, because lm-eval records how many documents it graded but never how many it attempted. That's the honest label — completeness is unknown, not established — but it applies fleet-wide until the producers record the count.

🤖 #8122 is merged (`fb91b3dc94`). #8084, #8085, #8086 and #8087 closed with it; leaving this thread open for whatever comes next.

What landed, briefly. Every eval score now carries an interval that covers the items its run did not grade, from one engine (`marin.evaluation.eval_stats`) that the producers and evaldash share. The estimand is fixed once — θ over the items a run set out to grade — and the unobserved part is bounded rather than imputed, so admitting a partial run costs interval width instead of quietly biasing the number upward. Every ordering sorts on the lower bound.

Two things worth knowing if you use the panel:

**evalchemy results are no longer "completeness unknown."** lm-eval publishes no attempted-item count beside its metrics, so the honest reading of every evalchemy run was sampling error with unknown completeness. Its per-sample rows do carry the document indices it enumerated, so the export pass that was already reading those files now derives the attempted count, the pass tally, and the count of items whose grader extracted no answer. That moves the fleet onto identified intervals.

**A benchmark where nothing parseable came back is held out of the panel** rather than standing as a model's newest score. The zero is real, but it is equally consistent with a broken grader, and publishing a collapse on that basis is the same error as hiding it. The cell reads `flagged` and links the run; `include_flagged=1` admits it.

Also folded in: Harbor's 90% infrastructure gate with its per-cause error counts, cross-cohort merge of the newest valid result per benchmark, benchmark-column selection with a one-action complete-panel filter, and `/api/compare` answering orderings with a difference interval instead of two error bars.

Not done, and the honest gap: comparisons are not paired on the items both runs actually graded. That needs a join across two sample archives per request. Worth filing when someone wants it.

The shared launcher defers task-catalog validation to the remote evaluator, so an MRCR request can allocate and serve a 67B model before discovering that the task is unavailable.

Reproduce:
1. Check out Marin commit `93251781092fa281077dff0a9c7b455fd6cc9677`, which pins Evalchemy commit `cf66d0b14975379bf7fc5c4a7cfff1400c636f1c`.
2. Request MRCR through a supplied Evalchemy config.
3. Observe that local launch validation succeeds, then the remote evaluator cannot resolve MRCR. Expected: Marin pins a reviewed evaluator containing MRCR's immutable dataset definition, grading metric, dependencies, and task-catalog tests. Local preflight rejects unavailable tasks before allocating inference capacity.

Experiment #8702 validated an MRCR implementation, but that implementation remains in unmerged PR #8706 and is unavailable from Marin's pinned evaluation path.

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The ragged EP expert MLP runs its six grouped GEMMs on vendored QuACK SM100 kernels (`sonic_cute`), MuonH's expert-stack Newton-Schulz uses QuACK's symmetric GEMM, and the FA4 segmented backward imports two QuACK layout helpers. Research branch [`research/mcwitt/xla-ragged-dot`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/xla-ragged-dot) replaces the expert MLP with three `jax.lax.ragged_dot` calls, whose derivatives produce the three activation-gradient and three weight-gradient grouped GEMMs, and removes every QuACK use from `moe_hero_ep`; fork branch [`marin-community/xla@mcwitt/ragged-dot-cudnn`](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/tree/mcwitt/ragged-dot-cudnn) (3 implementation commits, 59 lines) makes XLA lower them competitively on GB200. Upstream-preparation branch [`marin-community/xla@research/ragged-dot-astra`](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/tree/research/ragged-dot-astra) consolidates the same changes into two reviewable commits and adds rewrite, end-to-end numerical, and rematerialization regression tests. This issue tracks finishing that replacement.

Measured on one GB200 at the hero chunk shape (301,466 rows, 3 experts, latent 3072, intermediate 3072), whole expert MLP forward plus backward per chunk:

- XLA's fast path is cuDNN's MoE grouped matmul behind `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_fusion`. XLA requires cuDNN 9.22 or later and leaves this flag off by default; jax 0.11.1's hermetic cuDNN is 9.12, so the pinned PJRT wheel expands every ragged dot to a masked dense dot: 80.6 ms against QuACK's 28.2 ms. With the flag enabled, a wheel built against pip cuDNN 9.25.1.1 headers (`LOCAL_CUDNN_PATH`) fixes the forward and activation-gradient legs.
- The weight gradients (ragged-contracting mode) never reached cuDNN. cudnn-frontend 1.22 has `MoeGroupedMatmulBwd`; the fork branch maps that mode onto it. `MoeGroupedMatmulBwd` lowers to a cuBLASLt grouped GEMM that needs cuBLASLt 13.5 or later at run time (the repository's `uv.lock` pins 13.4.1) and writes its result column-major per expert, so the fork swaps the operands to land in XLA's row-major layout.
- With the experimental flag enabled, the cuDNN 9.25-built wheel, the contracting-mode lowering, and cuBLASLt 13.5 or later, all six GEMMs run on cuDNN and pass the QuACK numerical comparison: weight gradients are at performance parity (6.39 vs 6.40 ms), forward and activation-gradient legs reach 82 to 88 percent of QuACK's speed, and the whole MLP takes 34.1 vs 29.6 ms.
- At hero scale two further losses had to go: XLA's rematerialization pass recomputed the cuDNN custom fusions (1344 extra executions, 1.9 s per step) and the SwiGLU backward materialized a minor-axis concatenate (1.5 s per step). [`marin-community/xla@mcwitt/ragged-dot-cudnn`](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/tree/mcwitt/ragged-dot-cudnn) now excludes custom fusions from rematerialization, and [`research/mcwitt/xla-ragged-dot`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/xla-ragged-dot) projects gate and up with separate ragged dots.
- The upstream Triton ragged-dot emitter series (openxla/xla#45998 to openxla/xla#46002) was cherry-picked, built, and abandoned: wrong forward at unaligned group sizes and 14x slower weight gradients.
- The two-commit XLA series merges cleanly into `openxla/xla` main at `8eefa9f251` (2026-09-09). The [cuDNN weight-gradient commit](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/203a7cfc3b01e92b7f5bade9c031b21c470e1e9e) is suitable for a focused upstream PR: the original cuDNN work in openxla/xla#40189 left weight gradients on dense expansion, current `openxla/xla` main still lacks contracting lowering, and openxla/xla#45998 prefers cuDNN before its Triton fallback. It should remain behind the experimental flag because openxla/xla#43702 disabled cuDNN ragged-dot lowering after JAX failures with cuDNN 9.22 on H100 and B200, and openxla/xla#43307 tracks a Blackwell SIGSEGV. The [generic rematerialization commit](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/125086678cd93ff322ce45b3a6794d5b364ff4e4) should stay fork-local as written: it prevents every `kCustom` fusion, including cheap fusions, from being recomputed, while the rematerialization pass intentionally favors avoiding OOM over recomputation cost. An upstream version needs a GPU-provided eligibility predicate or an explicit per-fusion opt-out, with a cuDNN ragged-dot reproducer.

Hero measurement, one NVL72 rack, restore from hero step-54000, 55 scored steps, same night: QuACK control (`marin-community/marin@39f7f54cfe`) 24.84 MFU median, 265k tokens/s, peak 114.0 GiB; XLA ragged_dot (branch b49629532d, wheel `0.11.1+marin.7984f85e8ce6`, pip cuDNN 9.25.1.1 and cuBLAS 13.6.1.10) 23.77 MFU, 254k tokens/s, peak 109.7 GiB. Per-step losses agree to 5e-5 over the window and the 4-GPU ragged-EP dense-reference gate passes. W&B runs `rdx-ctl-a` and `rdx-cudnn-d` in `marin_moe`.

Open work:

- Two of four one-rack XLA/cuDNN runs hung silently (one after step 6, one before step 1: GPUs at 100 percent utilization near idle power, NCCL RAS clean, rank 0 blocked in the train loop). No QuACK run hung. Single-GEMM and degenerate-group microbenchmarks do not reproduce it. [`research/mcwitt/xla-ragged-dot`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/mcwitt/xla-ragged-dot) forwards `CUDA_*` env to the train tasks so a user-triggered GPU core dump can be armed for the next hang.
- The profile attributes the 1.06 MFU percentage-point gap versus the QuACK control to cuDNN's forward-shaped GEMMs and the unfused SwiGLU. The next planned optimization is a SwiGLU epilogue inside the cuDNN ragged-dot fusion.
- Rebase [`203a7cfc3b`](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/203a7cfc3b01e92b7f5bade9c031b21c470e1e9e), whose compatibility was checked at `openxla/xla@8eefa9f251`, onto `openxla/xla` main at PR preparation time. Run `RaggedDotFusionRewriterUnitTest.TestSupportedRaggedContractingDot`, `RaggedDotFusionRewriterIntegrationTest.TestRaggedWeightGradient`, and the hero-shape benchmark on H100 and Blackwell with cuDNN 9.22 and 9.25 where those combinations are available. Record results and unavailable matrix cells on this issue, and keep the lowering behind `--xla_gpu_experimental_use_ragged_dot_fusion`.
- Keep the blanket custom-fusion rematerialization exclusion in the Marin fork while preparing a separate design for a GPU-provided eligibility predicate or explicit per-fusion opt-out. Construct its cuDNN ragged-dot regression test so the unpatched pass produces two grouped-GEMM custom fusions after rematerialization and the fix leaves one.
- Landing needs a promoted fork wheel in `lib/marin/pyproject.toml`, direct minimums of `nvidia-cudnn-cu13>=9.25.1.1` and `nvidia-cublas>=13.6.1.10`, and exact resolved versions in `uv.lock`; `uv lock --upgrade-package` moved NCCL in one resolver attempt and was reverted. Current research runs inject these packages through `--pip-package`.
- The QuACK dependency stays until `moe_hero_fsdp`'s `sonic_cute` backend, MuonH's expert-stack Newton-Schulz GEMM, and the FA4 segmented backward's layout helpers are replaced.

Done when:

- `moe_hero_ep` runs the ragged expert MLP on `jax.lax.ragged_dot` with the promoted fork wheel and NVIDIA package minimums in `lib/marin/pyproject.toml`, exact resolved versions in `uv.lock`, and no `--pip-package` injection; optimized HLO contains the six expected cuDNN ragged-dot fusions.
- The hang has a linked reproducer and verified fix, or four consecutive one-rack NVL72 runs restore from hero step 54000 and complete the same 55-step scored window without a retry or stall.
- On the same dated allocation, median MFU over the 55-step scored window differs by at most one percentage point from the QuACK control, and the absolute loss difference is at most 5e-5 at every aligned scored step.
- The final pinned wheel passes the 4-GPU ragged-EP dense-reference gate.
- The `moe_hero_fsdp` `sonic_cute` backend, MuonH expert-stack Newton-Schulz GEMM, and FA4 segmented-backward layout helpers have tested replacements; `quack-kernels` is absent from `lib/marin/pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`.

issues.author: lukedhlee
issues.body:
**EAGLE-3 speculative decoding works on Snowball.** A first draft, trained in 25 minutes, decodes every stream 1.50× faster on held-out 64k R2E-Gym turns with the model's outputs unchanged. Sharing the pilot in case it is useful for GrugMoE inference; code, data and checkpoints are at the bottom.

Why decode is the target: RL steps are generation-bound — about 70 % of a 740 s step is the trainer waiting for rollouts, and a trajectory is 80 % LLM decode. Decode is the one part no other lever (staleness, admission, weight sync, grouped GEMM) touches.

Related: #5772 (MTP, closed), #7913, #7912.

**Why EAGLE-3, not MTP.** MTP was dropped in #5772: memory pressure on the target model, and the plan became "a draft trained *after* the main model (DSpark) if we need inference speedup". [EAGLE-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01840) could be a good alternative that is compatible with RL. Three things matter:
- Cheap to train: one Llama layer on the model's own outputs, 12 minutes per epoch on one node, nothing at pretraining time.
- One upfront cost, reused across RL: the draft is a separate model that weight sync never touches, and RL moves the policy slowly, so retraining could be occasional rather than per step (according to some RL people; one can measure this staleness curve).
- The model's outputs do not change (a rejected guess is replaced by the model's own token), so it is safe for on-policy RL.

**Pilot** (64k Snowball 67B-A2B, Jupiter GH200, production serving config, real 64k R2E-Gym turns, 17 node-hours total):

![Pilot draft on held-out 64k R2E-Gym turns: 1.5x per stream, turn latency down 38-47 %, 2.15-2.55 tokens per step](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/lukedhlee/17f11f75b7e68698ed701ef698f4fbb4/raw/pilot_speedup.png)

**The pilot works.** Served on held-out 64k R2E-Gym turns the draft never saw, 16 streams per node:
- Every stream decodes **1.50× faster** (139 vs 93 tok/s).
- A turn takes about half the time (median 11.5 s → 6–7 s).
- The node finishes **56 % more turns per minute**.
- Zero errors; outputs match the base server (two same-node repeats: 1.50× and 1.51×; sampled log-probs and top-1 mass match the no-draft runs).
- Long context did not hurt: 2.55 tokens per step accepted on prompts over 40k, 2.15 under 16k.
- This passes the gate set before training (≥ 2 tokens per step, long ≥ short, ≥ 1.4× per stream), from a first draft trained in 25 minutes.
- At 1.5× per stream the RL step should shrink about 19 % at fixed staleness.

Details:
- Extra cost of checking the draft's guesses when none are accepted: 1.33× per token at 16 streams/node (1.19× at 64).
- Best case with a perfect draft: 3.05 tokens per step at production sampling. So a good draft should give somewhere between 1.5× and 2.3× per stream, and cut the RL step by 19 % to 32 %. The pilot came in at 1.5×.
- Draft trained in 25 minutes on one node on 12k of Snowball's responses to SFT-corpus prompts, not RL rollouts (Snowball wrote the turns; the tool outputs in between are the originals from the SFT trajectories). R2E-Gym was held out.
- Room above: with this many guesses accepted, the simple formula expected 1.8×. We got 1.5× because checking guesses costs a bit more than we measured with none accepted. So two things raise the number further: a draft whose guesses are accepted more often, and a cheaper check.

**What can get even better.**
- The draft is small and quick (12k samples, 25 minutes of training). Train a bigger one on more of Snowball's outputs and more guesses get accepted, moving the 1.5× up toward the 2.3× best case.
- Checking guesses costs more than we measured with none accepted (that is why 2.2–2.5 tokens per step gave 1.5×, not 1.8×). Make the check cheaper and the same draft goes faster.
- Train the full draft on the pre-RL probe rollouts: we already run a probe over the whole task set before every RL run, and those rollouts are exactly the training data a draft wants, so the probe pays for itself twice.

**Risks.**
- Drift: as RL moves the policy, the draft's guesses get accepted less often. Serve the same draft against later checkpoints and see how fast acceptance drops; that tells us how often to retrain it (~3 node-hours).
- Context beyond 64k is untested.

**Code, if anyone wants to take over.**
- vLLM fork: https://github.com/lukedhlee/vllm/tree/lukedhlee/grugmoe-eagle3 (off the marin pin `fa50698a`). Four commits: [d84b7c7](https://github.com/lukedhlee/vllm/commit/d84b7c7b0) exposes GrugMoe's hidden states to a draft (`SupportsEagle3`); [a9ae5c9](https://github.com/lukedhlee/vllm/commit/a9ae5c9c3) stops a dense draft from doing the MoE's data-parallel sync every step (the cost fix); [4bb838c](https://github.com/lukedhlee/vllm/commit/4bb838c5e) and [4cfae4e](https://github.com/lukedhlee/vllm/commit/4cfae4ec8) fix vLLM's hidden-state extraction connector (it wrote scrambled dumps). Everything else is stock vLLM: `extract_hidden_states` to dump, `speculative_config={"method":"eagle3","model":<draft>,"num_speculative_tokens":3}` to serve.
- Trainer: https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators (`0.8.0.dev0`), with one commit on a fork so the training targets include GrugMoe's gated final norm: https://github.com/lukedhlee/speculators/tree/lukedhlee/grugmoe-gated-norm ([6496b4d](https://github.com/lukedhlee/speculators/commit/6496b4d)).
- Bench, corpus, extraction, validation and pipeline scripts: `/e/project1/transfernetx/lee27/code/snowball/bench/` on Jupiter; pilot data and checkpoint under `/e/data1/mmlaion/lee27/eagle3/` (`ds_pilot`, `ckpt_pilot/1`).

**What the next stage looks like**, for anyone who wants to pick it up or reuse the pieces: train the full draft on the pre-RL probe rollouts (no extra generation; ~20 node-hours to extract and train) → serve it against later checkpoints to see how fast acceptance drops → run one RL 2×2 ({14, 24 engines} × {base, draft}), log acceptance every step, and compare GPU-hours per accepted step with signals unchanged.
