issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
The ragged all-to-all EP backend hangs at the d6144 hero scale (11 racks, 704 GPUs) within the first hundred steps, on both attempts of the 2026-09-02 deployment. The train step never completes on one rack, the other ten spin in the next AllReduce, and levanter's progress watchdog kills the gang 15 minutes later (`No progress after train_step_started for 909.8 seconds (timeout 900.0); terminating with exit code 124`). No rank logs an error: nothing from NCCL, XLA, CUDA (no Xid), the allocator, or Kubernetes. The hero was rolled back to `04751985c7` (pooled-wave backend), which resumed cleanly from the same checkpoint.

Deployment: main `8e48cdb3ca`, run `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k` resuming `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` from its `step-54000` permanent checkpoint (#8868), `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, `--xla_gpu_experimental_ragged_all_to_all_use_device_kernel=true --xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`, jax 0.11.1, NCCL 2.30.7. Coordinator `/marin/hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step54k-coord-aade2815`; both attempts ran on the same 176 nodes.

- Attempt 0: steps 54001–54070 completed normally (loss tracks the pooled-wave run step for step at −0.006 nats, drops 3.4e-2 → <1e-4, MFU 20.5 → 23.4%, peak HBM 103.6 GiB). Step 54071 started at 00:23:30Z and never finished; killed 00:38:46Z.
- Attempt 1: restored the same checkpoint, completed step 54000 at 00:45:38Z (loss 1.2364, identical to attempt 0), then hung on step 54001; killed ~01:01Z.

Both hangs are on the first plain train step after a `diagnostic_watch_step` step (54070 → 54071 after seven clean alternations; 54000 → 54001 on the first). The plain and watch steps are two XLA executables that share the NCCL symmetric-memory arena for the ragged all-to-all: each registers its own window at the arena base (`AcquireSymmetricMemory`, `CollectiveMemoryCache`), and equal footprints coexist. #8861 is the same design failing the other way: an executable with a *different* footprint (the capacity-limited eval) makes the next train step fail with `ncclGroupEnd() failed: invalid argument`. Here the footprints are equal and the failure is a silent hang instead of an error, so #8859 (dropless eval only) removes the crash but not this.

Evidence that the hang sits on one rack's EP domain rather than a node fault:

- NCCL RAS (periodic `STATUS` from process 0, `telemetry_v1.levanter`): six minutes into each hang, 64 cross-rack communicators show an AllReduce operation-count skew of exactly 3 (attempt 0: min 10509 / max 10512 at 00:29:43Z; attempt 1: 190 / 193 at 00:52:30Z) and the 704-rank communicator a skew of 2. Before the hangs every communicator was in sync. One member per cross-rack communicator behind by the same count is one whole rack that never entered the step's trailing AllReduces.
- Iris per-task CPU (`iris.task`): exactly 16 of 176 tasks ran at ~4.0 cores while the other 160 ran at ~8.0 during each hang, i.e. one rack in a different wait state from the ranks busy-polling in AllReduce. Attempt 0: tasks 128–143 (zone 129, nodes `s38vxs64 s45sxs64 s51vxs64 s5xvxs64 s69vxs64 s7htxs64 s7qvxs64 s8ktxs64 s8mtxs64 s8yvxs64 s9jvxs64 s9lrxs64 scspxs64 scssxs64 sd8sxs64 shmsxs64`). Attempt 1: tasks 64–79, a different rack on the same node set.
- py-spy thread dumps (`iris process profile threads`) of tasks 0, 83, and 140 during attempt 0: every rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), no Python-side wait; the hang is below XLA's dispatch.
- No node conditions or events on either rack; the cluster's six `HPCVerification=Fail` nodes are elsewhere.

The stall-triggered verbose RAS capture (`trigger = stall`) published nothing in either attempt, so the rank-level view that would name the stuck ranks and the pending collective is missing; the periodic sample is all we have. Neither a 200-step 1-rack smoke restoring the same checkpoint (20 watch/plain alternations) nor the 11,420-step d768 rung reproduced it, so the failure needs more than one rack, i.e. more than one EP domain sharing the job.

Side observations from the same deployment: a cold compile at this shape took 22.9 min for the watch executable plus 6.6 min for the plain one; the data loader's second 64-item prefetch took 920 s (overlapped by compile) where the pooled-wave hero's restarts took under 100 s.

Done when: the ragged backend runs at 11 racks through at least several hundred steps with watch steps enabled without a hang, or the hang is reproduced at smaller multi-rack scale with a GPU-side stack (CUDA core dump / `cuda-gdb` on a stuck rank) that names the kernel or collective.

Related: #8861 (symmetric-window overlap between executables), #8859, #8868, #8506 (hero status log). Side-by-side trial report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/ep_change:-hero-ragged-a2a-swap,-200-step-trial--VmlldzoxNzg1ODIzMA==

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The mechanism this issue describes is not what the hung run did, and the root cause is still open. Recording what has been ruled out so the next attempt does not repeat it.

The hero had one train executable, not two alternating ones. `launch_scaling_ladder.py:216` sets `WatchMode.INLINE` at the deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca`, so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built (`train.py:906`), `jit_train_step` computes watch stats on every step, and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. Step 54071 was byte-identical to 54070 at the XLA and NCCL level. The working pooled-wave hero carries the identical watch config and does not hang.

The capacity-limited evaluator was already disabled. `c3f51e5250` (#8859) is an ancestor of `8e48cdb3ca`, and the dropless evaluator uses `sonic_cute`, which has no all-to-all and registers no symmetric window.

Window aliasing is present but was not the trigger. Two `jit_train_step` executables per rank each register a window at `0xbf80000000`; the cause is now known and is a step-counter sharding mismatch (details in #8861). What turns that aliasing into the `ncclGroupEnd` error is a third executable with a smaller footprint, and no such executable was running here.

Ruled out with evidence, all on one rack at the hero's shape, data and checkpoint unless noted. GIN: the device kernel logs `lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152 num_updates_per_replica=6`, and forcing `lsa_size < num_ranks` produces `Device kernel skipped: lsa_size=32 num_ranks=64 requires GIN` followed by a hard `RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed`, so `SupportsGin()` is false in this configuration. That also proves every hero EP domain was a single NVLink domain, since a domain spanning two would have failed loudly rather than stalled. CTA co-residency: the LSA barrier is per-slot, not grid-cooperative — `blockIdx.x` selects a barrier slot and CTA k rendezvouses only with CTA k on its peers — and at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)` the 152-CTA grid uses a fraction of the device, so `0de14631ea` did not regress residency and the comment in that patch claiming the whole grid must be resident is wrong. `core_count` divergence: every rank reports `cta_count=152`. Hardware: the task-index-to-node map is identical across both attempts and the two stuck 16-task slices share no node. Allocator address churn: `Buffer allocations changed address between module jit_train_step executions` fires only for `parameter` and `live-out` entries, never `temp`, so the arena backing the window is stable. Ragged metadata: `CheckRaggedAllToAllBounds` passed 160 of 160 checks on the same HLO operands the device kernel consumes. NCCL 2.31.2: tested, identical failure (see #8861).

One rack does not reproduce it. Attempts covered two 32-GPU EP domains in one rack (161 steps, clean), raised collective overlap (dies of NaN at step 2, which is #8317's corruption and a different regime), NCCL channel contention, forcing the GIN branch, and a full-fidelity control at 48 layers with mixture data restored from the same `step-54000` checkpoint. The remaining differences at eleven racks — cross-rack collectives sharing the GPUs, and a 704-rank communicator — cannot be built inside one NVLink domain.

What survives is a stall in the LSA barrier that cannot report itself. XLA calls `ncclLsaBarrierSession::sync` in the no-timeout form, and NCCL sets `abortFlag` only `if (isInternal)` (`src/dev_runtime.cc:1175`), so a user-created devComm has none and no watchdog, abort or CUDA error can fire. The barrier epoch is an absolute counter that persists across launches and is zeroed once at `ncclDevCommCreate`, so any divergence is permanent.

Three instrumentation gaps made both attempts undiagnosable, and should be fixed before the next one. The stall diagnostic is never wired: `train.py:968` calls `progress_watchdog.create(process_index=...)` with no `diagnostic=`, so `diagnostic_timeout` stays unset and the stall capture publishes nothing. If it were wired it would run on the wrong process, because `ProgressWatchdogConfig.create` returns `None` for the entire watchdog when `diagnostic_timeout` is set and `process_index != 0`. And the watchdog's `startup_grace_period` defaulted to one hour, which covered attempt 1's entire hang — that run was killed by hand, not by the watchdog.

For the next eleven-rack attempt: set `TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=0` alongside `TF_CPP_VMODULE=ragged_all_to_all_thunk=3,nccl_symmetric_memory=3,gpu_executable=5`, and `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG,INIT,COLL`. `TF_CPP_VMODULE` alone emits nothing, and `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` emits nothing for this failure class. A diagnostic PJRT build on `marin-community/xla` branch `mcwitt/8870-barrier-timeout` bounds both LSA barrier waits with NCCL's timeout overloads and records the stalled rank, barrier slot and phase, so the next occurrence names itself instead of producing fifteen minutes of silence. It also builds the device kernels against the NCCL the runtime loads: `tensorflow.bazelrc` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION=2.29.7` while the runtime installs 2.30.7, and the timeout API exists only in the newer headers.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up on one hypothesis worth keeping open: that this is the same class of bug as #8861, namely a sharding JAX infers rather than one the code specifies, going wrong only once `replica_dcn` is a real axis.

Partial test on one rack. A single rack can make that axis non-degenerate by splitting into several expert domains, so: `--expert-axis-size 32` (giving `replica_dcn=2`) with `--num-experts 192` to keep six local experts per GPU and the hero's memory profile, 48 layers, inline watch, with the #8861 step-counter fix applied. Result was 64 arena windows, 64 `jit(train_step)` compilations across 64 ranks, and a per-leaf `Format` diff reporting `identical across the step`. No second state-sharding mismatch appears when the replica axis becomes real, and the #8861 fix holds there.

That does not close the hypothesis. It covers the train state only, at replica width 2, inside one NVLink domain and one process group. It does not cover batch sharding over `_BATCH_AXES = ("replica_dcn", "data", "expert")`, intermediates inside the step, or device ordering across 704 devices in 176 processes. Ordering is the part that matters here: `compact_grug_mesh` builds the mesh by reshaping `jax.devices()` in process order, while a `GSPMDSharding` carries the client's default device order, and the two coincide trivially when `replica_dcn=1`. A disagreement that resolves differently on different racks is the only proposed source of rank-dependent behaviour that survives, which is what a failure hitting one rack of eleven — a different one on each attempt — requires.

The direct test is a dump comparison, and it was not possible before now. `hero_grug_trainer_config` left `sharding_dump_path=None`, so `dump_grug_state_sharding_run_artifact` wrote to the pod-local `logs/` directory and the hung run's dump died with its pod. The ladder now writes it under the run's output path, so the next multi-rack run leaves a dump that can be diffed against a one-rack dump directly. That needs no special build and costs nothing.

Also worth recording for anyone reproducing this: `--expert-axis-size 32` at the hero's 384 experts puts twelve local experts on each GPU instead of six and OOMs at 158 GiB. Halve the expert count to hold the per-GPU profile fixed.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 An eleven-rack reproduction attempt on 2026-09-03 did not reproduce the hang, but it eliminated data- and state-dependence by direct measurement and turned up a version skew that reframes the failure. Root cause is still open.

**The reproduction was faithful, and it did not hang.** Two jobs at 11 racks, 235 steps in total (164 then 71), restored from the same `step-54000` both failed attempts used, at the hero's exact shape. It matched attempt 0's loss to ±0.00007 nats over the whole overlapping range and sat -0.0058 nats against the pooled-wave control, reproducing the -0.006 offset reported above; MFU 22-23% against attempt 0's 23.4%. It carried the same transport (`lsa_size=64 num_ranks=64 gin=false cta_count=152`) and the same symmetric-window aliasing this issue describes: 1408 arena-window registrations across 704 ranks, exactly two per rank, alongside 1408 `jit_train_step` compilations.

**The hang is not a function of the data or the model state.** Attempt 0 completed step 54071 (`train_loss` 1.23687 at 00:23:35.14Z) and hung on the next one. The replay ran through that step and kept going. Since the loss agrees to seven significant figures, the batch, the routing, the optimizer state and the arithmetic there are identical to the run that died. Combined with attempt 1 hanging at 54001 from the same restored state, the trigger is timing, not state, and the failure cannot be forced by choosing a checkpoint or a step.

**On the statistics, stated carefully.** Hero exposure was 75 step-attempts with two hangs; the reproduction ran 235 clean. A one-sided test gives p ≈ 0.06 — suggestive that something differs between the two setups, but not significant. Job-steps are the right unit here, not rack-steps: the hang is a job-level event, so counting all 11 racks as independent trials overstates the evidence.

**Candidates eliminated since the last update.** Concurrent checkpoint I/O: `grep "Saving checkpoint"` across every task log in both attempts returns zero hits, so neither attempt ever wrote a checkpoint. Online W&B: per-step tracker cost was 3.73-3.84 ms at every detail step and the wandb thread was idle in `selectors.select` at the py-spy dump. The NCCL RAS probe: it ran in both attempts at a 600 s cadence taking 69-83 ms, and the 00:29:43.8Z poll *succeeded during the hang*, so process 0 and NCCL's in-process listener were responsive while the gang was wedged. A rank silently falling off the device-kernel path: `RaggedAllToAllThunk::RunCollective` returns `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")` when `xla_gpu_allow_ragged_all_to_all_nccl_send_recv_fallback` is false, which is the deployed setting, so such a rank fails loudly rather than desynchronising quietly, and no attempt logged an error. Two ragged kernels sharing barrier slots: the hero forces `--xla_gpu_experimental_parallel_collective_overlap_limit=1`, so collectives cannot be co-resident.

**The version skew, which is a real defect on its own.** `tensorflow.bazelrc:192` pins `HERMETIC_NCCL_VERSION="2.29.7"` while the runtime resolves to 2.30.7. NCCL's `ncclDevCommCompat_v22907` shim then forces `ginType = NONE` and gates `deviceApiSupport` on `ncclTeamLsa(comm).nRanks == comm->nRanks`. That explains structurally why `SupportsGin()` is false — it was never a configuration choice — and why the device kernel only ever runs on the per-rack EP64 clique, so eleven racks are eleven independent barrier domains whose hazard adds with rack count while nothing couples them. It also means the deployed kernel is compiled without 2.30's bounded `sync(..., timeoutCycles)` overload and without its system-scope release fence in `arrive`, which is exactly why the stall cannot report itself.

**Leading remaining hypothesis.** A stray peer store from the copy loop landing inside the devComm resource window and corrupting the barrier state. Every symmetric window, including the one holding the barrier epochs, lives in the same `devr` VA reservation with a common `stride4G`, and the barrier epoch is an absolute per-slot counter that is never reset or exchanged, so any divergence is permanent: a peer that falls behind makes its partner spin on a comparison that wraps to ~2^32, with `abortFlag == nullptr` for user devComms and no timeout. One sub-case has a matching upstream fix we do not carry: NCCL `0d7243b`, "Mitigate loadConst `__ldg` regression", replaces the non-coherent `__ldg` read of `lsaFlatBase`/`stride4G` with a plain dereference, and those window pointers are rewritten at run time by `ncclDevrReplaceSegmentWindowsIfNeeded`.

**Instrumentation now exists, and did not before.** `CUDA_` was missing from the dispatcher's forwarded env prefixes, so the GPU core-dump variables could never reach a training gang; with that fixed the driver creates one dump pipe per rank. A dump must be taken with `CUDA_COREDUMP_GENERATION_FLAGS=skip_abort,skip_global_memory,skip_constbank_memory`: the default writes 62 GB and SIGABRTs the process, which killed all 64 ranks of a smoke gang and lost the dump with the pod, while the flags give 283 MB. Even so it is terminal within about two minutes (measured at 2:36 and 1:55), so it must trigger, read and upload in one round trip and go last. A dump taken mid-kernel names the resident kernel and gives a per-block state table, which matters because the LSA barrier is per-slot indexed by `blockIdx.x` and that table therefore names the diverged slots directly. NCCL RAS `VERBOSE STATUS` can also be triggered by hand during a hang, answering in ~4 ms with the per-collective min/max that showed the AllReduce skew of exactly 3. Do not attach `cuda-gdb` to a live process: an attach to PID 1 returned nothing in 150 s and took the gang down.

**Next.** A wheel built with the device kernels compiled against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7 exists as `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-ca0716a2da95`; it removes the skew, adds bounded LSA barriers that record rank, slot and phase, extends the bounds check to the device path, and promotes the transport line to INFO. It is being validated on one rack. The one structural difference between the hero and the reproduction that survives all of the above is that the hero runs `broadcast_one_to_all` inside `checkpointer.on_step` on every step — a cross-host collective on a `(176, 4)` mesh whose rank groups exist nowhere else in the job — while the reproduction, with `save_checkpoints=False`, never creates a checkpointer at all (`train.py:1031`). A next window should restore that at zero I/O cost with `--save-checkpoints --checkpoint-minutes 600`, and a one-rack `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,REG` A/B on that flag would first confirm the communicator inventory actually differs.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 One actionable gap found while testing a prediction of the barrier-stall hypothesis, worth recording separately because it is cheap to fix and independent of everything else above.

The hypothesis predicts the stuck rack's GPUs were saturated during the hang, spinning inside a resident device kernel, as opposed to idle because the kernel never launched. That is directly checkable from `iris.task`, which carries `accelerator_util_pct` and `accelerator_mem_bytes`. During attempt 0's hang window (00:23:36-00:38:43Z) **both fields are null in all 2,636 samples**.

The query is sound: the same rows reproduce the known CPU signature exactly, with the stuck rack at 4.04 cores against 7.85 on the healthy racks, matching the 4.0-vs-8.0 split reported in this issue. So the nulls are a collection gap rather than a query error.

That gap is expensive out of proportion to its size. GPU utilisation separates "spinning in a resident kernel" from "kernel never launched" on its own, which is the first branch any analysis of this failure has to take, and it needs no core dump, no rebuilt wheel and no reproduction. Enabling accelerator telemetry on the hero gang is the cheapest single change that would improve the next occurrence.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Follow-up with the experimental record from the overnight session. Four more mechanisms eliminated, three of them by direct experiment rather than inference, and two of them hypotheses raised in this issue's earlier comments. Root cause still not determined; what follows is what a next attempt should not spend time on.

**Residency starvation is refuted.** The concern that the ragged kernel's grid cannot stay fully resident is real in principle — the LSA barrier makes CTA k wait on CTA k of every peer, and a CTA that is never scheduled stalls its peers forever, while the already-resident CTAs spin holding their SMs and never yield, so nothing can free what the missing CTAs need. The pre-patch wheel `marin-xla-pjrt-20260828-c9526e8c0272` is maximally exposed to this: it sizes the grid as `kGridSmMultiplier * core_count` where `kGridSmMultiplier = kRaggedAllToAllDeviceKernelCtasPerSm = 8`, i.e. 1216 CTAs against exactly 1216 CTA slots at `__launch_bounds__(128, 8)`. Zero headroom, and its own comment states the requirement. Run at hero shape on one rack it completed **176 steps, roughly 8,400 ragged launches each needing all 1216 CTAs resident simultaneously, with no stall**. Foreign occupancy during the ragged kernel is therefore effectively zero and starvation at the shipped wheel's 8x margin is implausible.

Incidentally, that wheel is about 11% faster: 16.4 s/it and 23.8% MFU against the shipped 18.3 s/it and 21.5%. The grid patch buys a margin this result suggests is not needed, which is worth revisiting on its own merits.

**The autotune-cache race is not this.** The shared node-local `/cache/xla/per-fusion-autotune` race (#8896) is real and caused a hero retry, but it cannot reach the train step: a 40-step run at a never-compiled shape wrote **zero** autotune results, because this model's heavy GEMMs are Marin's own CUTLASS kernels rather than XLA-autotuned fusions. Autotuning fires only for incidental ops such as the checkpoint slice, so divergent results there cannot change the train step's fusion selection, buffer assignment, arena size or window registration.

**Cross-rack GDR cannot corrupt the barrier.** `devr->lsaFlatBase` is a dedicated `cuMemAddressReserve`; NCCL's network buffers are separate `ncclCudaCalloc` allocations registered through `ncclNetRegMr`. A NIC can only write inside a registered memory region, and a write outside it is rejected by hardware with a completion error rather than landing silently elsewhere.

**Divergent devComm Requirements would be the cleanest mechanism, and both routes to it are closed.** Two ranks requesting different `Requirements` get different devComms, hence different barrier buffers, and since devComm creation is collective each would wait in a barrier the other never joins — silent and permanent, needing no epoch divergence at all. But divergent `lsa_size` takes the `has_remote_peers && !SupportsGin()` branch and fails loudly with `InvalidArgument("RaggedAllToAll fallback to NCCL is not allowed")`, and no hero rank logged an error; while divergent `core_count` would be a static per-node property, and the failure moved between two node sets the forensics established are disjoint.

**The kernel's copy loops are bounded.** Both the LSA loop and the inner copy terminate on `num_lsa_updates` and `hi` respectively, `hi` is clamped to each update's own extent, and the GIN branch is dead in this build. Combined with the eliminations above, the barrier is the only place this can hang — that part is now established by construction rather than inference.

**Reproduction attempts, all null:** eleven racks at hero shape (235 steps); maximum executable churn with four executables cycling (~300 steps); registration determinism (all 64 ranks byte-identical, 29 registrations, same order and offsets); cold autotune at a novel shape; zero-headroom residency (176 steps); four EP cliques on one rack (189 steps); and a second transfer geometry at `--latent-dim 2048 --capacity-factor 1.37`, which changes stride and alignment in every offset the copy computes (192 steps).

A single rack cannot reach the remaining space, and the reason is structural: symmetric windows are registered only by the ragged path (`--xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`), so extra communicators and expert-domain splitting do not emulate eleven racks. Closing this needs the failure state observed. The capture path is now armed by default on the ragged transport, so the next occurrence should name itself rather than produce fifteen minutes of silence.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Correction to a recommendation I left in an earlier comment. I suggested a one-rack A/B on `--save-checkpoints` to confirm that the hero's per-step `broadcast_one_to_all` creates a communicator inventory the reproduction lacks. I have now run it, and that test cannot work on one rack. Anyone picking this up should not spend a window on it.

Ran at hero shape with `--save-checkpoints --checkpoint-minutes 600`, which exercises the collective without ever performing the 5.4 TB write, and with the step-sharding fix disabled: 164 steps, 16.9 s/it, no stall.

The reason it is not a real test is in the counter. `Init COMPLETE` appears **64 times, once per rank — a single communicator**. At one rack the `(16, 4)` process mesh *is* the same 64 ranks as the expert-parallel clique, so `broadcast_one_to_all` reuses that communicator and creates no distinct rank group. At eleven racks the mesh is `(176, 4)` and spans all 704 ranks, so its rank groups exist nowhere else in the job. The structural difference I wanted to probe only exists at multi-rack, so a clean single-rack result says nothing about it either way.

That matters beyond this one experiment, because it closes the single-rack search on structural grounds rather than by exhaustion of ideas. Two independent reasons now, both measured:

- Symmetric windows are registered only by the ragged path (`--xla_enable_nccl_symmetric_buffers_for_collectives=raggedalltoall`), so additional communicators and expert-domain splitting add no window pressure and do not emulate eleven racks.
- The last identified per-step difference, the checkpointer's `broadcast_one_to_all`, collapses onto the expert-parallel clique at `(16, 4)`.

Note also that `save_checkpoints=False` means no checkpointer object is constructed at all (`train.py:1031`), so every reproduction attempt in this issue executed that collective exactly zero times. That remains the only per-step structural difference between the configuration that hung twice and the ones that did not — it simply cannot be tested below eleven racks.

Nothing here changes the standing conclusion: the locus is established (the kernel's copy loops are bounded, so the barrier is the only place this can hang) and the unreportability is explained, but the trigger is undetermined and needs the failure state observed. The capture path is armed by default on the ragged transport, so a recurrence should name itself.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Retitled from "hangs on one rack at d6144 hero scale after a watch step" to drop the watch-step attribution, which the evidence no longer supports.

The original framing was that two executables — a plain train step and a `diagnostic_watch_step` — alias the symmetric-memory arena, and that the hang lands on the first plain step after a watch step. The deployed commit sets `WatchMode.INLINE` (`launch_scaling_ladder.py:216`), so `_make_diagnostic_watch_step` is never built: `jit_train_step` computes the watch statistics on every step and `step % 10 == 0` only decides whether the host logs them. The hanging step was byte-identical to the step before it.

The timing correlation is also weaker than the title implied. With `HERO_WATCH_INTERVAL = 10`, attempt 1 completed step 54000, a watch-boundary step, and hung on 54001 — immediately after. But attempt 0 completed **54071** and hung entering 54072, two steps past the 54070 boundary. One attempt fits the pattern and one does not, so "after a watch step" is not a property of the failure.

Worth keeping from the original framing: there really are two executables per rank sharing one arena, and that part is confirmed at hero scale (1408 arena-window registrations across 704 ranks, exactly two per rank). The cause is not the watch step but the step counter's inferred sharding, which is #8861's root cause and is fixed on `mcwitt/8870-repro`. Whether that aliasing is also what makes this issue's hang possible is still open.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Result of the 2026-09-04 eleven-rack telemetry window. No hang in 183 job-steps, but the new barrier instrumentation produced the first *measured* asymmetry between racks this issue has had, and it is not hardware.

**What ran.** `mcwitt/8870-repro` @ `0ee0880b77`, which is the hung commit `8e48cdb3ca` plus diagnostics and nothing else (not rebased; the six main-line commits past `8e48cdb3ca` touch no training code). PJRT wheel `marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-3091aa7302d8`: device kernels built against the run-time NCCL 2.30.7, both LSA barrier waits bounded at ~45 s with a record naming rank, slot and phase on expiry, and — new for this run — a per-thunk, per-phase high-water mark of the barrier wait, logged at INFO whenever it doubles above 1 ms. Hero-identical otherwise: the #8861 fix switched off so both aliasing windows are present (confirmed two per rank), the checkpointer constructed with a 600-minute interval so its per-step `broadcast_one_to_all` runs, `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,NVLS`, core dump armed. Restored `step-54000`, 11 racks / 704 GPUs / batch 11264, system priority. Steps 54000–54183 at 17–19 s/it and 23% MFU, loss 1.2364 at 54000 exactly as in both hero attempts. Zero barrier timeouts, zero bounds violations, zero errors. The JAX compilation cache hit with the new wheel, since the cache key does not include the PJRT build (`cache_key.py` hashes `jaxlib`'s version and `platform_version`, which is the CUDA runtime), so startup was six minutes.

**The measurement.** Post-copy waits never exceed 4.2 ms on any rank. Pre-copy waits on racks 0–7 (tasks 0–127) never exceed 10.5 ms, with per-rack medians of 5.6–9.9 ms. Pre-copy waits on racks 8, 9 and 10 (tasks 128–175) reach **158, 103 and 128 ms**, with per-rack medians of 157, 98 and 124 ms — i.e. essentially every rank on those three racks saw it. Full sweep of all 704 ranks is in `scratch/8870/window/w3-waitmarks.csv`.

**Event structure.** Collapsing the ≥50 ms lines by timestamp gives six events during the run (a seventh at 23:31:46 coincides with the cancel at 23:31:50 and is teardown). Each is a single launch on a single rack in which **63 of the 64 ranks wait the same ~N ms** — so one rank arrived late to the pre-copy barrier and its 63 clique peers waited for it. The rank that did not wait is the straggler, and it is a different rank on a different node every time:

| time (UTC) | rack | waiters | median wait | rank that did not wait | node |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 22:36:36 | 9 | 63 | 98 ms | task 145 rank 3 | `s4gwxs64` |
| 22:36:56 | 8 | 63 | 101 ms | task 136 rank 2 | `s8mtxs64` |
| 22:37:29 | 10 | 63 | 81 ms | task 168 rank 2 | `s9jyxs64` |
| 22:38:33 | 8 | 45 | 52 ms | (19 below threshold) | — |
| 22:40:30 | 10 | 63 | 124 ms | task 162 rank 3 | `s2grxs64` |
| 22:45:18 | 8 | 63 | 158 ms | task 134 rank 3 | `s7qvxs64` |

Roughly steps 2, 2, 3, 8, 13 and 28. Six different nodes, six different ranks, three racks, never racks 0–7. A bad GPU or host would recur on itself; this roams. And these are sticky maxima that only log on a doubling, so a repeat at the same magnitude is invisible — the true event count is at least this and probably higher.

**Placement.** The task-to-node map was identical to the hero's own 176-task placement and to last night's second window; the first window differed at rack indices 0 and 1, so the index is "whichever racks are free" and is not a stable identifier. What is stable: rack 8 here is **the same sixteen nodes, 16 of 16, as the slice that stalled in hero attempt 0** (tasks 128–143, `s38vxs64 … shmsxs64`), and racks 9 and 10 were the same physical nodes in every one of these placements too. So this data cannot separate "the last three replica indices" from "these three specific racks". Against the hardware reading: attempt 1's stuck slice (tasks 64–79, rack 4) shows nothing here, 7.6 ms maximum, indistinguishable from the healthy racks.

**Reading it, carefully.** Pre-copy is the rendezvous before any peer store, so a long pre-copy wait means EP-clique peers had not yet *reached* the ragged kernel; the copies themselves are not slow (post-copy is flat). One rank per event arriving 80–160 ms late, recurring, only on replica indices 8–10 of the 11-wide `replica_dcn` axis, points at something rank-order-dependent upstream of the all-to-all: the two `nranks 11` replica-axis communicators that rank 0 reports (ring or tree position of the last three replicas), the data loader's per-replica shard timing, the checkpointer's `(176, 4)` broadcast that was live for the first time in a reproduction, or host-side work that lands on those ranks. None of that is tested. What it is not: a hang — 160 ms is three orders of magnitude short of 45 s, and in 183 steps nothing grew toward one. Whether the hang is the extreme tail of this distribution or a different phenomenon is exactly the open question, but until now there was no distribution to speak of.

**Also recorded from this run.** Communicator inventory on rank 0 with the checkpointer live: `nranks 64`, `704`, and two `nranks 11`. Two arena windows per rank (1408 across 704 ranks), as in the hang. `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=REG` was dropped after measuring that it alone produced 98.5% of task-log volume (one `IPC reuse buffer` line per collective per peer, 356 MB per task per hour, ~63 GB per window into finelog); without it a task logs ~5 MB. The hero resumed from the forced `step-61806` at 23:35Z and is running.

**Next.** (1) Make recurrence measurable: a per-launch histogram, or reset the marks every N launches, so the event rate and its trend over a longer run are observable rather than inferred from doublings. (2) Separate position from hardware: a placement that lands different physical racks at replica indices 8–10 — the Kueue gate that blocked today's smoke (#8925) makes this awkward but it is the decisive test. (3) Catch the straggler in the act: a host-side timestamp around the ragged thunk on every rank would say what the late rank was doing — the barrier marks say only that it was late. (4) Repeat with the #8861 fix on, to see whether one executable per rank changes the tail.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The hung run pinned a QuACK version with a concrete matrix-multiplication (GEMM) scheduler defect. This is a new lead; the cause of #8870 remains unproved.

The deployed commit `8e48cdb3ca` [pins QuACK 0.6.1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/pyproject.toml#L96), and the archived attempt-0 task-1 setup log confirms `quack-kernels==0.6.1`. The ragged backend's [activation GEMMs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e48cdb3ca/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/_moe/sonic_cute.py#L57) use Cluster Launch Control (CLC), which lets resident GPU thread blocks take over work from pending clusters, with variable-length expert groups. The audited package source matches the [0.6.1 release](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/02c7f69881737731173a6a009aeb6f032e449b61/quack/tile_scheduler.py#L504).

That scheduler can observe a failed CLC cancellation, leave its work loop, and then issue more cancellations through its unconditional `cancel_pending_tail` path. NVIDIA's [PTX specification](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/archive/13.0.0/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#parallel-synchronization-and-communication-instructions-clusterlaunchcontrol-try-cancel) defines further cancellation requests after a GPU thread block observes failure as undefined behavior. The drain also issues asynchronous requests without waiting for their responses before exit.

Upstream [58cb592a1a6e](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6e) replaces this path with a conditional, response-checked drain and a separate response buffer. Its [investigation](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/blob/58cb592a1a6e/AI/clc_spurious_invalid_investigation.md) reports stale GEMM output tiles with a second process sharing the GPU and multiple queued GEMM launches, plus a separate GPU-error hazard from requests still in flight at block exit. Those experiments used B300; they do not establish the behavior of our GB200 run. The specification violation does not prove it caused our silent hang, and the cached GPU binary from the original run has not yet been checked against that source.

If this defect prevents a rank's GEMM from completing, the other ranks in its expert-parallel group could wait indefinitely at the next ragged barrier. The [earlier bounded-copy-loop argument](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5537281960) does not exclude a preceding kernel that never completes. Next is a comparison of the original scheduler and a narrow drain fix under finite competing GPU work, checking for incorrect outputs, timeouts and GPU errors at the production matrix dimensions. Each version will use a separate compilation cache so the treatment executes newly compiled code.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The [QuACK scheduler lead](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5548674783) now has a GB200 output-corruption reproduction. In a four-GPU comparison, the original scheduler left output regions unwritten in three cases with a competing process. The narrow drain fix and the no-Cluster-Launch-Control (no-CLC) control had no detected errors.

| Arm | Quiet cases passed | Contention cases passed | Measured launches |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Original QuACK 0.6.1 | 3/3 | 1/4 | 12,080 |
| Narrow upstream drain fix | 3/3 | 4/4 | 21,000 |
| No CLC | 3/3 | 3/3 | 18,000 |

Each case used a fresh process and isolated compilation cache, BF16 constant inputs, 16 queued GEMMs with distinct outputs, and synchronization before reset and validation. The contender ran matrix multiplications in a separate process on the same GPU. Original and fixed arms each repeated one contention case on a different GPU, accounting for their fourth case. The failures occurred on three different GPUs; all incorrect elements retained the output's sentinel value. An independent harness audit found no reset, aliasing, layout or numerical-reference error explaining the retained sentinel values. The three tested shapes were synthetic; this initial comparison did not use the original run's recovered three-expert dimensions. Passing cases reached 3,000 launches after 3.59–16.92 seconds of measured work. Failed cases stopped at their first bad batch, so aggregate counts do not estimate a long-run failure rate.

The historical binary audit also found the unsafe drain in four of the nine CuTe cache keys logged by the original attempt-0 task-1, representing three distinct binaries. Original cache objects predate the run and match the audited bytes in the historical snapshot spanning its lookups. This establishes historical cache contents, rather than an independent dump of the hung process's GPU memory.

The connection to the silent training hang remains unproved: these failures returned incorrect outputs without timing out. A repeat is running with dimensions recovered from the original saved config and source, using synthetic balanced routing. A same-process competing-stream test will address the difference between this reproduction and the training workload. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/340) preserves the evidence boundary and experiment constraints.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The production hero — on the **pooled-wave** transport, not ragged — stalled silently for fifteen minutes today and then died of an NVLink fault, and it originated on one of the three racks the telemetry window flagged. This is the strongest evidence so far that #8870's root cause is a fabric fault on specific NVL72 domains rather than anything in the ragged kernel, which merely fails silently where NCCL's host path eventually fails loudly.

**Timeline (2026-09-05, UTC), `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` on the same 176 nodes and the same rack map as both 09-02 hang attempts and the 09-04 window.** Last step 65069 completed at 17:19:31. Nothing was logged by any rank for the next fifteen minutes; Iris's py-spy dumps at 17:21 and 17:31 show every sampled rank's main thread inside `train_step` (`train.py:1176`), i.e. blocked on the device — the #8870 shape exactly. At **17:34:36.549 task 162 rank 1 on `s2grxs64` (rack 10, NVLink domain `dh1-r137`)** logged the first `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over nvlink or a hardware error` (from `cudaFreeAsync`, `gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:414`); the other rack-10 nodes followed within 0.5 s, racks 2 and 6 by 17:34:37.8, and every rack by 17:34:43 — 88 of 176 tasks logged the fault, the rest were taken down by fate sharing. Iris restarted the gang; it resumed from the hourly temp `step-64944` at 17:38, so the event cost 125 steps plus 20 minutes. It is healthy again (step 65623 at 20 s/step).

**Why this bears on the ragged hangs.** The pooled-wave transport moves data through NCCL's host-driven path, where a fabric fault eventually surfaces as a contained CUDA error and the driver tears the context down. The ragged device kernel spins in an LSA barrier with `abortFlag == nullptr` and, on the wheel that hung, no bounded wait, so the same fault produces fifteen minutes of silence followed by the 900 s progress watchdog — which is what both 09-02 attempts looked like. The fifteen-minute latency before the contained error is itself notable: the fault was in progress, invisible, for as long as the ragged hangs lasted before the watchdog fired.

**The three racks now line up with three independent fabric observations.** Rack 10 (`dh1-r137`): today's fault origin; and `s2grxs64` is the node that supplied the 22:40:30 straggler in the window (task 162, 124 ms). Rack 8 (`dh1-r129`): the 09-02 attempt-0 stall node set; a 5.009 s NVLS multicast bind at window startup (9-12× every other rack); the only repeat straggler node; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 is a flapping NVLink — 505 recovery events lifetime, +3 in a 21-minute sample last night and +1 more since, read-only from the running hero, the only counter that moved anywhere in a five-rack sweep. Rack 9 (`dh1-r136`): stragglers in the window, no counter evidence yet. Racks 0-7 show none of this. Rack 10's own GPU-side link counters did not move across today's fault, so the error is on the switch side or a non-link hardware error; node `dmesg`/XIDs are not visible from inside the containers.

**What this changes.** The 09-04 deep-dive (`scratch/8870/window/deepdive/`, eleven streams) had already falsified the cross-rack collective-stall mechanism and left "a per-GPU transient of 25-160 ms, ≥11× more frequent on racks 8-10, with nothing upstream of the GPU to blame." A fabric fault that stalls whatever is crossing a link, escalating occasionally to a contained error or a permanent stall, fits every measurement in this issue, including why attempt 0 hung on rack 8 and why one-rack reproductions on healthy racks never reproduced anything. It does not explain attempt 1 (rack 4, `dh1-r124`), which shows nothing in any sweep; that may be a fourth domain or a different event.

**Untested but now less likely as the cause:** the NCCL 2.29.7/2.30.7 compile skew (the ragged wheel that hung compiled its kernels against 2.29.7; every diagnostic wheel since used 2.30.7). It remains the one code difference between the hung configuration and every clean run, and an A/B wheel exists (`marin-xla-pjrt-candidate-355d8f15cc25`), but today's fault happened with no ragged kernel in the picture at all.

**Asks.** (1) Infra: node-level `dmesg`/XID history and fabric-manager/NVSwitch logs for `dh1-r137` around 17:19-17:35 today and `dh1-r129` around 2026-09-04 22:35:04-09; and `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 as a flapping link. (2) Before the next ragged deployment, a pre-flight that reads NVLink error counters and times the first symmetric-window bind per rack, and refuses racks that stand out. (3) The next 11-rack window should run the per-node 1 Hz GPU/NVLink sampler now on the branch (`MARIN_DEBUG_GPU_SAMPLER_SECONDS=1`) with the per-launch barrier reports, so a link recovery and a barrier stall can be joined at one-second resolution.

Data: `scratch/8870/window/hero-20260905-fault-ranks.txt` (first fault per task/rank/node), `gpuhealth{,2,3}/` (three read-only counter sweeps).

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body: 🤖 The [QuACK upgrade branch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/upgrade-quack-064) includes the [upstream CLC scheduling fix](https://github.com/Dao-AILab/quack/commit/58cb592a1a6ef85a69e37d0b4eb50217b59d20ca). comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The September 9 production stall adds evidence for a timing-sensitive synchronization failure after a slow data fetch. This is a hypothesis; the blocked GPU operation and root cause remain unknown.

The affected attempt was `hero-ragged_a2a-ep-step81k-coord-1515615f`, with 176 tasks and 704 GPU processes. Its setup logs on tasks 94 and 149 report `quack-kernels==0.6.4`, so this recurrence does not support treating the QuACK upgrade as sufficient to prevent hangs. All times below are UTC on September 9.

- Step 81,758 completed at 19:59:39.838 with loss 1.2321685553. No later completed step was retained for this execution.
- At 19:59:50, all 704 processes reported a data fetch taking at least 10 seconds. Subsequently 680 reported at least 20 seconds, 271 at least 30 seconds, and 19 at least 40 seconds. The final warning was at 20:00:20.119. These counts use distinct task/local-rank pairs.
- Retained Python stack captures at 20:09:40–20:09:54 cover all 704 training processes: every main thread was in `train_step` at `moe_hero_ep/train.py:1176`, and every data-prefetch thread was waiting to enqueue into a full queue. This argues against an ongoing data-loader wait as the condition sustaining the stall. Python stacks do not identify the executing GPU kernel.
- NCCL RAS snapshots at 20:07:56 and 20:17:56 show unchanged AllReduce count ranges of 6,238–6,241 across 64 communicators, plus a range of 10,822–10,824 on one communicator. Both snapshots reported all ranks present, with no missing, unresponsive, or considered-dead ranks across 76 communicators; no communicator records were omitted or invalid. Persistent count divergence does not establish that NCCL caused the stall: an earlier GPU operation can prevent a rank from reaching the next collective.

A candidate trigger is unequal rank arrival after the slow fetch exposing a synchronization defect in the ragged collective or another GPU operation. The warnings describe background prefetch, and per-rank fetch-completion and train-step-entry timestamps are missing, so they do not establish that the delayed fetch fed the stalled step. The earlier [NVLink fault evidence](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) remains relevant; this observation does not exclude hardware or fabric faults.

The discriminating test is a controlled replay with selected ranks delayed before a training step, comparing ragged A2A with the alternative pooled-wave expert-communication backend and capturing per-rank entry times plus verbose RAS and GPU/native stacks if it stalls. That test has not run.

The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) preserves the attempt/execution identifiers and Finelog query scope for the retained evidence.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Audit of the eleven-rack evidence as of September 9, 22:21 UTC: the NCCL 2.30.7 header build is a promising mitigation, but the record does not support treating all four clean windows as tests of that change. My subjective confidence that the header update materially reduces or resolves the specific ragged-A2A hang is about 60%; this is an engineering judgment, not a statistical posterior or a claim that the failure is eliminated.

Installation logs and distinct process-zero `train_loss` steps give this corrected inventory. Counts include the completed step carrying the restored step number; the earlier comments reported slightly smaller counts at their observation cutoffs.

| Eleven-rack run | PJRT build | Compiled NCCL headers | Completed step records | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| September 3, `ra2a-8870-w1-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 165: 54000–54164 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w2-hero11` | `e94a45d2a446` | 2.29.7 | 72: 54000–54071 | No recorded hang |
| September 4, `ra2a-8870-w3-hero11` | `3091aa7302d8` | 2.30.7 | 185: 54000–54184 | No recorded hang; instrumented wheel |
| September 9, production attempt `72aad6e7` | `b183c591142c` | 2.30.7 | 217: 81716–81932 | Still progressing at the cutoff |

All four used NCCL runtime 2.30.7. The verified newer-header exposure is therefore 402 completed steps across two runs; 237 additional clean steps used the old headers. The earlier statement that every clean reproduction used newer headers was incorrect. The [first two windows](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5534213125) also omitted the checkpointer's per-step broadcast. The [third window](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5547757908) restored that broadcast but added bounded barriers, wait instrumentation, initialization waits and post-collective device-to-host copies. Its success cannot isolate the header change.

Today's run is stronger evidence. It has 176 running tasks, 704 GPU processes, PJRT `b183c591142c`, NCCL runtime 2.30.7 and QuACK 0.6.4. The wheel's source change from production's `3a8f3392723e` is the two-line NCCL build-default update in [XLA PR #22](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/pull/22). The live `train.py` hash matches main, and the batch-ready host barrier is absent. The preceding production attempt `1515615f` used PJRT `3a8f3392723e` with NCCL 2.29.7 headers and runtime 2.30.7; it completed 43 steps from the same restored step 81716 before stalling. Today’s wheel omits the September 4 diagnostic barrier timeouts and device-to-host wait-record copies. This is useful evidence against those diagnostic copies or the proposed host barrier being necessary for the current improvement. It is still one uninstrumented success, with build toolchain, allocation and timing differences, rather than a randomized wheel A/B or a tested restart sequence. Old-header clean windows and the [September 5 pooled-wave run’s contained NVLink error](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8870#issuecomment-5554893088) keep alternatives credible; that separate failure shows hardware can also cause a similar stall.

There is also preliminary numerical and performance evidence. Comparing today’s run with `1515615f` over matched steps 81726–81758, loss differed by at most 0.000110 nats, with mean treatment-minus-control +0.0000076. The mean of the reported `throughput_mean_mfu` samples was 21.626% for the new wheel versus 22.110% for the earlier attempt, a decrease of 0.484 percentage points (2.19% relative). These 33 matched steps are observational and do not establish a performance regression or non-regression. Sustained training and restart validation remain open.

For reproducibility, the historical execution IDs are `iris:227df97f1c61d78c`, `iris:8a8e59dcdce56776` and `iris:153389937ce684a7`; today's control and treatment are `iris:a8d3026cb58a0341` and `iris:aa61bafbfdef1160`. Counts use `levanter.metrics`, `name='train_loss'`, `process_index=0`, deduplicated by execution and step. The Marin hub lagged today's regional metrics: 196 records through 22:13:27 UTC on the hub, with the remaining 21 through 22:21:17 UTC verified on `cw-us-east-08a`. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/378) and [wheel-pin PR #9062](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9062) track the current mitigation.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 The source audit found two concrete deadlocks in the remote GIN branch, but neither explains the measured `gin=false` hero path. Zero-size updates skip completion signals that the receiver still counts. Separately, receiver CTA0 can snapshot a shared signal after another CTA's current-launch sends arrive, then wait for an unreachable count. Both predate [3a8f3392723e](https://github.com/marin-community/xla/commit/3a8f3392723e321d806012c5aab492a73bd194c3); these are independently checked protocol schedules, not GPU reproductions.

No missing local CTA synchronization was found in the executed LSA branch: NCCL already joins CTA threads before release publication, and kernel completion joins the matching peer-copy barriers. That result depends on valid metadata, matching grids, serialized barrier resources and CTA progress. It does not locate the original blocked operation. A preceding GEMM or stalled peer-memory transaction can strand peers at the next ragged barrier; the earlier finite-copy-loop argument does not exclude either.

Fresh Finelog analysis confirms larger checkpoint-adjacent dips. Across 1,567 intervals between successive completed-step timestamps per arm (each labeled by its ending step), ragged had eleven intervals above 1.5× its 17.598-second median, all within checkpoint state step through step+4; pooled-wave had one above 1.5× its 19.610-second median. Watch-boundary concentration remains unconfirmed: stalled steps were 54072, 54001, 81759 and 83308, plus three first-step failures after restore. Same-day old-header attempts hung after 43, 0, 0 and 0 completed steps; the new-header trial ran about 300 steps before cancellation and the release hung after roughly 1,590. This is an apparent improvement in exposure before failure, not a controlled failure-rate estimate.

The upstream review found no change to the device-copy/barrier implementation from fork base `dcf304bc5d` through main `5718ca7411` (September 10, 17:11:56 UTC). [52a0596243](https://github.com/openxla/xla/commit/52a05962435a168467cc9f8443d3f83a14cbe2af), which explicitly prevents a deadlock, only changes one-shot debug bounds checking, outside the selected device path. The [incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/385) now includes the source audit, assumptions, query scope and discriminating measurements. The next decisive capture is the first blocked GPU operation plus per-rank/CTA barrier epochs and stream dependencies. A non-hanging run cannot identify the initiating blocked operation.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
Follow-ups for the TaskTrove Clean pipeline (#9061) from the dropped-source review, the six 100-task Docker samples and the 190-task end-to-end validity sample (Sonnet solve scripts executed on Daytona, ten tasks per converter). Each item is a defect in the data or a pool of tasks the pipeline could recover.

**Oracle run inside the container as a conversion-time gate for repository tasks.** The in-process checks cannot run pytest, and the validity sample found 3 of 10 swe_patched oracles scoring 0 in their own image: pennylane-2591 fails 3 of 132 graded tests with the shipped patch, pytensor-1056 grades node ids parametrized for macOS (`[...-Darwin]`), qiskit-terra-8924's test package imports `ddt`, which the image does not ship (the oracle's own pip step installs it only sometimes). Two more were tool or converter bugs, now fixed (node ids relative to a `tests/pytest.ini` rootdir; PASS_TO_PASS ids truncated at a space inside a parameter). A gate that builds the image and runs the oracle once per SWE task at conversion would reject the rest.

**nl2bash format ambiguity and seeded fixtures.** Six of ten nl2bash candidates scored 0 because the expected output is the oracle command's exact record stream (one word per line from `tr`, a NUL-separated list) while the instruction only names what to print; task_2493's oracle itself scores 0 because `setup_seeds.sh` creates a 200,000-byte file with `truncate` and the expected output is 16,666 lines of `sample_line`. Either the instructions pin the output format or the checker compares record sets.

**Judge sampling against a real model.** 379,356 judge tasks (272,429 with a reference, 105,875 rubric-only, tagged `reference` and `rubric`/`no-reference`) have only been exercised through the tool's `infra_error` path because no judge endpoint exists for the project (no Anthropic key in Secret Manager; `OPENAI_API_KEY` version 2 answers 401). Once an endpoint exists: run the validity sample's 30 judge tasks, then a larger stratified judge sample, and decide whether the rubric-only sources earn their place.

**Recoverable pools rejected by shape, not quality.** 22,863 structured-outputs tasks asking for xml, toml or csv (no mode); 12,453 non-Python swe_rebench repositories (Go, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust; `junit`/`gotest` modes exist but no converter); 3,607 MCQA tasks whose gold is not an option letter; 1,463 MCQA prompts with literal `\n` sequences; 282 reasoning-gym `arc_agi`/`rearc` tasks whose scorer in reasoning-gym 0.1.25 cannot score its own gold.

**Dedup policy for rubric sources.** Dedup is by identical instruction within a source: half of `nemotron-gym-safety-v3` (44,182 of 89,066) and nine tenths of `stackexchange-tezos` (`tezos-0340_copy1..9`) fall out. The safety copies may carry different rubrics; decide whether instruction-level dedup is the right key for judge sources.

**all-puzzles answer form.** Three of ten candidates had the right words but wrote them as a comma-separated list where the expected value is a list literal; the instruction should state the form or the checker should accept both.

**Packaging.** A PyPI release of `tasktrove-verify` so Dockerfiles install a pinned wheel instead of a git SHA (today any tool change is a new dataset version), and a Hugging Face upload of the clean dataset with the manifest and report.

**Validity tooling.** `validity.py solve` lost 4 of 190 calls to `claude -p` hanging past the 600 s cap (now a per-task error, not a batch abort); a retry with a fresh session and a lower cap would recover them.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** follow-up tracking list, not a single fix — analysis only, no PR.

This issue is nine distinct workstreams layered on the still-open, unmerged [#9061](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9061). The whole pipeline lives on `tasktrove-conversion-pipeline`; nothing is on `main`. Any fix here would depend on that branch, so these should each land as their own PR against `#9061` (or after it merges), not as a parallel change to `main`. Several items are new features or research questions (oracle gate, non-Python converters, judge sampling, packaging) that are individually >100 lines and multi-module. The right move is to split this into tracked issues rather than one PR.

**Research (grounded in the branch):**

- Grading runs in the `graded` step ([`verify.py` per README](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/tasktrove-conversion-pipeline/experiments/post_training/tasktrove/README.md)), which dedups then drops tasks whose grader doesn't hold up. An in-container **oracle gate** (build image, run the shipped patch once per SWE task, reject if it doesn't score 1.0) is a new sub-stage here, not a converter tweak. This is the highest-leverage item and gates the swe_patched/swe_repo pools.
- **nl2bash** already reimplements the oracle's multiset record comparison and fixes the seed-path bug ([`nl2bash.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/tasktrove-conversion-pipeline/experiments/post_training/tasktrove/converters/nl2bash.py)). The remaining 6/10 failures and the `setup_seeds.sh` `truncate` case are a format-contract decision: pin the output format in the instruction, or relax the checker to a record-set compare. Design call, not a bug.
- **Dedup policy** for rubric sources overlaps existing open issue [#9058](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9058). The key is instruction-level within a source ([`dedup.py` `dedup_key`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/tasktrove-conversion-pipeline/experiments/post_training/tasktrove/dedup.py)); the question is whether safety-copy rubrics differ enough to warrant a rubric-aware key. Consolidate this item into #9058.
- **Recoverable pools** are new converters/relaxations routed through [`registry.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/tasktrove-conversion-pipeline/experiments/post_training/tasktrove/converters/registry.py) (structured-outputs xml/toml/csv modes, non-Python swe_rebench, MCQA gold/`\n` normalization, reasoning-gym arc pin). Each is its own converter PR following the README's five-step recipe.
- **Judge sampling**, **PyPI packaging of `tasktrove-verify`**, **HF upload**, and the **validity `solve` retry** are blocked on external resources (a judge endpoint / Secret Manager key, a release, a bucket) or are ops tasks, not code changes landable from here.

**Proposed approach:**
- [ ] Split into separate tracked issues by workstream; fold the dedup item into #9058.
- [ ] Sequence the code items behind #9061 merging: (1) oracle-gate sub-stage in `graded`, (2) recoverable-pool converters, (3) nl2bash format decision.
- [ ] Track judge-endpoint provisioning, `tasktrove-verify` release + HF upload, and the validity retry as ops follow-ups.

Holding here for a maintainer to confirm the split before any implementation, since the target branch is unmerged.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
ToolScale v4 stores task-specific `FIXTURE`, `CATALOG`, and `CANDIDATES` data in `environment/toolscale_runtime.py`. Its Dockerfile copies that file to `/usr/local/bin/toolscale`. Harbor's Daytona `auto_snapshot` path names snapshots from a hash of every relative filename and file content under `environment/`, so every ToolScale row creates a separate snapshot even though the Dockerfile and runtime implementation are shared.

A full scan of the 4,048-row `laion/toolscale-v4` TaskTrove Parquet found one Dockerfile and 4,048 distinct Harbor environment hashes. After excluding the three serialized data assignments, the runtime source is byte-identical across all rows; the data contains 10 catalog variants. Across the current 1,739,326-row TaskTrove collection, ToolScale accounts for 4,048 of 4,125 snapshot hashes. The other sources use 77 hashes, so one shared ToolScale environment would reduce the expected total to 78.

Move the task-specific fixture data to a runtime-uploaded location such as `/setup_files/toolscale_fixture.json`, and have the shared ToolScale executable read it there. Harbor uploads `setup_files/` before agent setup. Preserve the existing `toolscale catalog`, `toolscale inspect`, and `toolscale call` interfaces. Preserve the verifier contract: calls append to `/app/toolscale_calls.jsonl`, and `/tests/check.py` requires the expected calls and evidence IDs plus the literal assertions in `/app/response.md`.

Done when:

- ToolScale tasks share one image or snapshot build input when their generic runtime is unchanged.
- Each trial receives its own catalog, candidates, fixture-backed calls, and evidence IDs before the agent starts.
- The verifier still requires the expected calls, evidence IDs, and response assertions.
- Tests cover two tasks with different fixtures and confirm that they share the environment hash while returning their respective task data.
- Regenerated ToolScale tasks no longer place task-specific runtime contents under `environment/`.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:

Marin consumes Harbor only as a pinned external dependency and, per the documented [ownership boundary](docs/harbor-integration.md#L121-L136), "does not install or import Harbor, `harbor_config`, Daytona, or Harbor's path runtime." The pin lives in [`marin.external_dependencies.HARBOR`](lib/marin/src/marin/external_dependencies.py#L64-L71) (`github.com/marin-community/harbor`, commit `ce2a5594`) and [`config/external/harbor/pyproject.toml`](config/external/harbor/pyproject.toml#L18-L19). The only Harbor code in-tree is the launch/policy shim under [`lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/`](lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/harbor/dataset.py) and the config catalog in `experiments/evaluation/`; the marina [`tasktrove`](infra/marina/apps/tasktrove/) app is a read-only corpus browser, not a task generator.

The pieces the "Done when" criteria require changing — the ToolScale task generator that writes the `laion/toolscale-v4` TaskTrove Parquet, `environment/toolscale_runtime.py`, its Dockerfile, Harbor's Daytona `auto_snapshot` environment-hash naming, `/setup_files/` upload ordering, and `/tests/check.py` — are all owned by the Harbor repo. None exist here, so there is no in-repo change to make and no meaningful test to add.

**Recommendation.** Refile this against `marin-community/harbor` (or move it), where the ToolScale runtime, Dockerfile, and Daytona snapshot path can actually be edited. I'm not opening a PR here. If you expected a Marin-side change (for example a policy or config adjustment under `experiments/evaluation/configs/harbor/`), point me at the concrete file and I'll scope it.

issues.author: jenna-russell
issues.body: I'd like to see how the uncheatable ai portion is influencing overall loss numbers. on a sample of historical uncheatable checkpoints, ive found that a lot of recent data, about 1/3, is AI, heavily dominated by ai code. From the checkpointed times uncheatable uploaded to huggingface, it seems that more and more of the evaluation is generated content on the material. I would like to understand how this affects evaluation. Our hypothesis is that AI will have a much lower loss, which could 'outweigh' any plateau or increase in human-written text loss. Thanks to @dlwh, we have some initial results after getting the document level loss on two uncheatable eval checkpoints on the Marin snowball run, one from September 2025 and one from July 2026. I've uploaded results to this google drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1pdD8AG3rzBG94iccQrcpAUX_t5uPF2N4?usp=sharing What we see: In September 2025, both macro and micro results are as expected (AI loss is much lower). In July 2026, the macro results show the oposite trend, but looking into this more it seems this is due to barely any humans writing code themselves anymore. When I switched to micro loss, we see that the loss is much lower for AI. The micro loss does seem to be converging more. Next step - we would want to look at many checkpoints within the Snowball run to see if we can cleanly separate out the human content loss from ai generated loss. Pangram is willing to supply research credits to continue this investigation! If anyone has any hypothesis or thoughts on a) whether we should optimize on AI-generated text performance at all and b) if so, how much would you want to 'weight' AI-generated text's importance compared to human text, please let me know.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body: this is super cool! My suspicion is that we do want to understand AI synthesized text since consuming agent-written text is becoming pretty common for agents (at least for us while coding). I guess in an ideal world where everything weren't causal modeling we'd learn to understand but not synthesize. We could maybe use a prefix tag to accomplish something similar?

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
We cannot trend NVLink link health on `cw-us-east-08a`. One link failed on 2026-09-10 after five days of visible warning, and the only record of that warning came from a hand-run sweep that no pipeline can reproduce.

On 2026-09-10 08:08:46 `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 reported `Xid 149, NETIR_LINK_DOWN Fatal XC0 i0 Link 14`, and CoreWeave moved the node to `production-reboot` at 08:09:21. #8934 had named that same GPU and that same link five days earlier. Three read-only `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` sweeps covering 320 GPUs on five racks, 18 links each, found every NVLink error counter at zero except one: link 14 on this GPU, which held 505 lifetime link-recovery events and was still incrementing, by 3 during a 21-minute sample and 1 more later that day. The written prediction preceded the failure and named the exact link. All 16 nodes of rack 129 faulted; `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 was the only GPU reporting Xid 149, the other 63 reported the downstream Xid 145, and it was the only node CoreWeave evicted.

The counters behind that prediction reach no dashboard or query. `gpu_nvlink_errors` and `gpu_health_status` have zero rows in every cluster across all retained history. CoreWeave's `dcgm-exporter` config requests all four `DCGM_FI_DEV_NVLINK_*_ERROR_COUNT_TOTAL` fields, but DCGM on driver 595.71.05 emits no samples for them, confirmed by scraping `:9400/metrics` on `s9jvxs64` directly. The four specs at `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/node_agent/kubernetes.py:427-454` are dead, and the `infra/grafana/dashboards/accelerators.json` panels that read them are blank. `..._COUNT_TOTAL` is also a per-GPU sum: per-link counts live in `..._COUNT_L0..L17`, which nothing requests, so no pipeline can attribute a fault to a link even if the fields were populated.

We do not need the exporter fixed to collect this. `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` reports per-link counters from inside a pod, and `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/gpu_sampler.py` on branch `mcwitt/8870-repro` (commit `6beb5ce640`) already samples it per node once a second. That code is not on `main` and has no pull request.

`s9jvxs64` is back in production and eligible for the next gang. CoreWeave placed it on hold, ran their L12 qualification, and returned it to `production` at 09:15:31Z; the node labels record `flcc.coreweave.com/previous-state=hold` and `last-seen-test-state=l12-test`. It carries no Iris pod as of 2026-09-10 20:37Z and has logged no Xid since 08:09:32Z, but it has also carried no NVLink traffic in that window, and nothing in Iris placement holds it out of the next job. The reboot most likely zeroed its counters, so the measurement that settles this is whether link 14 starts climbing again once the node takes load.

This is a tail-risk item on a healthy fleet. Two rack-scale NVLink episodes in 28.3 days of retention, across 208 GB200 nodes and 12 NVLink domains, is 5.9e-3 per rack-day. Scaling Meta's published Llama 3 405B figure of 4.74e-4 unexpected interruptions per GPU-day ([arXiv:2407.21783](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783) section 3.3.2) to 832 GPUs predicts 6.6 unexpected interruptions over our 404-hour steady-state window; we saw 8, of which 3 were hardware. Training availability over the last 338 hours is 96%. Nothing here shows a degrading fleet, and the work below is worth about a day.

Two open questions sit with CoreWeave and do not block the work. Whether their L12 qualification reads link-recovery counters, since this link passed it hours after failing. And whether racks 129, 137 and 394 run NVSwitch firmware older than 35.2015.4718, which NVIDIA documents as fixing Xid 149 on GB200 NVL72 by disabling the NVLink L1 low-power state ([known issues](https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgxgb200nvl72-release-notes/known-issues.html)).

Hardware attribution is only nine days deep. The `k8s/disruption` collector that carries node, rack and Xid identity merged on 2026-08-23 in #8601 and produced its first row on this cluster on 2026-09-01. Xid never reaches task logs. We cannot say whether these faults are new.

Done when:

- Per-link NVLink recovery counters are collected on `main` and queryable, without depending on CoreWeave's exporter config.
- The four dead specs and the Grafana panels that read them are fixed or removed.
- Link 14 on `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 has been observed under load, and either climbs again or reads flat.

Related: #8934 (the original fault report, closed in favor of this issue), #8912 (telemetry collection gaps), #8925 (Kueue lack-of-fit prevents moving a gang off a suspect rack), #8870 (the ragged-EP hang, attributed mainly to NCCL header skew in #9062).
issues.title: [infra] Collect per-link NVLink counters and watch s9jvxs64 link 14 under load

issues.author: mcwitt
issues.body:
Two GB200 NVL72 domains on `cw-us-east-08a` show fabric-level faults that have now cost the production hero a restart and are the leading explanation for the ragged-EP hangs in #8870. Filing separately because the asks are infrastructure-side and independent of any Marin code.

## 1. `dh1-r137` (rack index 10 in every hero placement): contained NVLink fault took down the hero

2026-09-05 17:19:31Z: `hero-wd-gate-router-p02-step58k` completed step 65069 and then stalled silently for fifteen minutes with every rank blocked on the device. At 17:34:36.549Z task 162 rank 1 on **`s2grxs64`** logged `CUDA_ERROR_CONTAINED: Invalid access of peer GPU memory over nvlink or a hardware error` (`gpu_cudamallocasync_allocator.cc:414`); the seven other nodes of the domain followed within 0.5 s (`s5k62nb4`, `s24qxs64`, `s91qxs64`, `s1zsxs64`, `s3ztxs64`, `s92vxs64`, …), and every rack within 7 s via fate sharing. The gang restarted from the hourly checkpoint; cost 125 steps plus 20 minutes. GPU-side NVLink error counters on the domain's 64 GPUs did not move across the event (read-only `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` before and after), so the fault is switch-side or a non-link hardware error. `dmesg`/XIDs are not visible from the task containers.

## 2. `dh1-r129` (rack index 8): a flapping NVLink and a 10× slow multicast bind

- **`s9jvxs64` GPU 0, link 14: 505 link recovery events lifetime, +3 in a 21-minute sample (01:53-02:13Z) and +1 more by 21:30Z**, while the production hero ran on it. Across three read-only sweeps of 320 GPUs × 18 links on five racks it is the only NVLink error counter that moved at all; every symbol/Rx/discard counter on every link is zero.
- At the start of the 2026-09-04 eleven-rack window, this domain's first NVLS multicast bind (`symTeamObtain`, between `NVLS Created Multicast group nranks 64` and the first `cuMulticastBindAddr`) took **5.50 s against 0.44-0.63 s on the other ten racks**, uniform to ±8 ms across all 64 GPUs — an excess of 5.009 s, a round five seconds, i.e. a timeout-then-succeed in a fabric-side path. One-shot; the second bind was normal.
- This is the exact node set (`s38vxs64 … shmsxs64`) on which the ragged hero stalled in #8870 attempt 0 on 2026-09-02.

## 3. What the training-side telemetry adds

The 2026-09-04 window's per-launch barrier-wait marks (see #8870) show one GPU per rack arriving 25-160 ms late at a random layer's all-to-all, ≥11× more often on rack indices 8, 9 and 10 (`dh1-r129`, `r136`, `r137`) than on the other eight, with nothing upstream of the GPU to blame (communicators, host, data loader and step-entry skew all measured flat). A link retrain stalls whatever is crossing the link for tens to hundreds of milliseconds, which is that shape.

## Asks

1. Node-level `dmesg`/XID history and fabric-manager / NVSwitch logs for `dh1-r137` around 2026-09-05 17:19-17:35Z and for `dh1-r129` around 2026-09-04 22:35:04-09Z.
2. Diagnosis of `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 (and its switch port); it is still recovering under load.
3. A per-rack NVLink health signal Iris can read before placing a gang (recovery-event rate, or a first-bind timing probe), so a known-bad domain is not handed to a 704-GPU hero. Placement is deterministic here — these domains have held rack indices 8-10 in every hero and window placement since 09-02 — so the same hardware keeps landing under the same job.

Related: #8870 (the ragged hang this most likely explains), #8925 (Kueue gate that prevents choosing racks), #8912 (Iris does not record accelerator telemetry).

The other exclusions were 16 nodes for CPU and one for memory; these counts do not prove that the reservation is the only capacity blocker.

Two corrections to this issue that #9086 records: the `dh1-r129`/`dh1-r136`/`dh1-r137` rack indices cited here are from the 2026-09-04 placement and no longer hold, since r393 left the fleet and r394 replaced it; and the 505 link-recovery figure came from a hand-run `nvidia-smi nvlink -e` sweep, which no telemetry pipeline can currently reproduce, because `gpu_nvlink_errors` has zero rows in every cluster.

comments.author: mcwitt
comments.body:
🤖 Closing in favor of #9086, which carries this evidence and narrows the follow-up to what we can act on.

What held up from this report: `s9jvxs64` GPU 0 link 14 failed on 2026-09-10 at 08:08:46Z with `Xid 149, NETIR_LINK_DOWN Fatal XC0 i0 Link 14`, five days after this issue named that GPU and that link. The prediction preceded the failure and named the exact link, and it remains the strongest evidence in the thread.

What did not hold up. The claim that fabric faults are the leading explanation for the #8870 hangs is too strong: the NCCL header bump in #9062 cut the hang rate from 4 hangs in 4 attempts to 1 in roughly 1900 steps, and the two failure modes have since separated cleanly. The rack indices 8, 9 and 10 cited here are from the 2026-09-04 placement and no longer map to `dh1-r129`, `r136` and `r137`, because r393 left the fleet and r394 replaced it. Section 3's statement that communicators, host, data loader and step-entry skew were "all measured flat" overstates the source comment, which listed them as untested candidates. `s8wvxs64` is not a repeat NVLink offender: its 2026-09-01 eviction was `NetworkAlertFault=IBFlappingSingleNodeInterface`, which is InfiniBand, and membership in the 15-node rack-394 taint set says nothing about which node was the source.

The fleet-wide rate does not support an infrastructure escalation. Two rack-scale NVLink episodes in 28.3 days across 208 nodes and 12 NVLink domains is 5.9e-3 per rack-day, at or below the rate implied by Meta's published Llama 3 405B figures scaled to this fleet, with 96% training availability over the last 338 hours. Hardware attribution is also only nine days deep, since the `k8s/disruption` collector produced its first row here on 2026-09-01, so no trend claim is available either way.

CoreWeave has already qualified and returned the node: it went to hold, passed L12, and was back in `production` at 09:15:31Z. The open asks in this issue are superseded by the narrower work in #9086, which is collecting per-link counters ourselves so the next occurrence is measured rather than swept by hand.
